x ↦ fθ(x) ↦ ŷ  ·  three parts, nineteen sections, one machine
Convention. Colour in this lecture is never decoration. Every box, arrow and symbol is tinted by what kind of quantity it is, and that mapping never changes.
data Activations — anything computed forward from the input.  x, h(l), ŷ
params Learned parameters — the only things gradient descent may change.  W, b, θ
loss The scalar objective and the error signal at the output.  L, ŷ − y
grads Gradients — anything travelling backward.  ∂L/∂W, δ(l)

Solid arrow = forward computation. Dashed arrow = gradient. A dotted box = an object that is tied (reused) somewhere else — the single most important idea in §4–§8.

We are handed n examples drawn i.i.d. from an unknown joint distribution p(x, y):

D = {(xi, yi)}i=1n,   xi ∈ ℋd,   yi ∈ 𝒫

Three choices define a learning problem, and only the third and the shape of 𝒫 change between regression and classification:

  • Hypothesis class ℱ = {fθ : ℋd → 𝒫 } — what functions we are willing to consider. This is the architecture.
  • Loss ℓ(ŷ, y) → ℋ≥0 — the price of predicting ŷ when truth is y.
  • Risk — what we actually want small: R(θ) = 𝔼(x,y)∼p[ℓ(fθ(x), y)]
The catch. p is unknown, so R is not computable. Everything downstream is a workaround for this one fact.

Since p is unknown, replace the expectation by its Monte-Carlo estimate on the sample we do have:

R̂(θ) = 1n n∑i=1 ℓ(fθ(xi), yi)
θ⋆ = arg minθ R̂(θ) + λ Ω(θ) (ERM)

By the law of large numbers R̂ → R as n → ∞, but for finite n the gap R − R̂ is the generalisation error — which is what λ Ω(θ), the regulariser, is there to control.

Everything today is this. §2–§8 only ever change fθ. The optimisation template — take gradients of R̂, step downhill — is fixed from here on.
Fixed for the whole lectureChanges every section
the objective R̂(θ) the hypothesis class ℱ — i.e. the architecture
gradient descent on θ which parameters are shared, and along which axis
the loss family (§1) how far information travels in one layer
The three-way decomposition
𝔼[R(θ̂)] − R⋆ = εapp▁▁▁architecture + εest▁▁▁finite data + εopt▁▁▁SGD stopped early

Choosing an architecture is choosing how to trade εapp against εest. A CNN has higher approximation error than an MLP of the same width — it simply cannot represent some functions — but far lower estimation error on images, because its hypothesis class is smaller and better aimed.

Read this as. "Inductive bias is not a limitation you tolerate; it is the term you are buying."

This single trade-off explains every arrow in the roadmap: each one shrinks the hypothesis class using a true fact about the data (pixels are local, time is ordered, tokens relate pairwise) and is rewarded with better generalisation from the same n.

Problem. 𝒫 = ℋ (or ℋk). Predict a continuous quantity: a price, a pose, a temperature, the next value of a signal.

Squared-error loss

ℓ(ŷ, y) = 12(ŷ − y)2 the ½ is bookkeeping — it cancels on differentiation

Why squared error and not |ŷ − y|? Two reasons, one statistical and one practical:

  • It is the MLE under Gaussian noise. Assume y = f(x) + ε, ε ∼ 𝒩(0, σ2). Then maximising ∑ log p(yi | xi) is minimising ∑(ŷi − yi)2.
  • Its minimiser is the conditional mean. arg minc 𝔼[(c − y)2 | x] = 𝔼[y | x] — so a well-fit regressor estimates the mean of the target distribution.
  • It is smooth everywhere, so gradients are defined and Lipschitz; |·| is not differentiable at 0.

The flip side: squaring makes the loss dominated by outliers. When that hurts, swap in Huber (quadratic near 0, linear far out) — the model does not change at all, only ℓ.

Problem. 𝒫 = {1, …, K}, an unordered finite set. "Cat" is not 2.7 and is not between "dog" and "car".

The honest loss is the 0–1 loss, which just counts mistakes:

ℓ0-1(ŷ, y) = 1[ŷ ≠ y]
But. It is piecewise constant: gradient zero almost everywhere, undefined at the jumps. Minimising it exactly is NP-hard. It is useless to optimise.

So we do two things. First, predict a distribution rather than a label: p̂ ∈ ΔK−1, the probability simplex (p̂k ≥ 0, ∑k p̂k = 1). Second, minimise a differentiable surrogate — the negative log-likelihood of the true class, a.k.a. cross-entropy:

ℓCE(p̂, y) = −log p̂y = −K∑k=1 yk log p̂k

Cross-entropy is a calibrated surrogate: minimising it also minimises the 0–1 risk. It is convex in p̂ and unbounded above, so being confidently wrong is punished hard.

Regression headtorch
head = nn.Linear(d_model, 1)      # -> R
loss = nn.MSELoss()               # 1/2 (y_hat - y)^2, averaged
y_hat = head(h).squeeze(-1)
L = loss(y_hat, y)                # y: float tensor (B,)
Classification headtorch
head = nn.Linear(d_model, K)      # -> logits, not probabilities
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()      # log_softmax + NLL, fused
logits = head(h)
L = loss(logits, y)               # y: long tensor (B,) of class ids
ŷ = fw,b(x) = w⊤x + b = d∑j=1 wjxj + b

Absorb the bias. Append a constant 1 to every input and a slot to w, so the model is purely linear and the algebra stays clean:

x̃ = (1, x1, …, xd)⊤,   w̃ = (b, w1, …, wd)⊤  ⇒  ŷ = w̃⊤x̃

Stack the n examples into a design matrix X ∈ ℝn×(d+1), one example per row:

X = — x̃1⊤ — ⋮ — x̃n⊤ — ,  y = y1⋮yn  ⇒  ŷ = Xw
Note. "Linear" means linear in w, not in x. Replacing x by any fixed feature map φ(x) = (1, x, x2, sin x, …) keeps every formula on the next slide verbatim. This is exactly what §3 makes learnable.

Objective

J(w) = 12 ‖Xw − y‖22 = 12(Xw − y)⊤(Xw − y)
Why this is easy. J is a convex quadratic in w: its Hessian X⊤X ⪰ 0 everywhere. A convex function has no local minima, so ∇J = 0 is necessary and sufficient for a global optimum.

This is the only model in the lecture with that property. From §3 onward J is non-convex and ∇J = 0 merely means "some stationary point" — which is why we switch to iterative methods and never look back.

Two matrix-calculus facts used below
∇w(a⊤w) = a,    ∇w(w⊤Aw) = 2Aw for symmetric A

Derivation

J(w)= ½(w⊤X⊤Xw − 2y⊤Xw + y⊤y) expand; the two cross terms are equal scalars ∇wJ= X⊤Xw − X⊤y apply both facts; last term is constant ∇wJ= X⊤(Xw − y) = X⊤r factor — note the residual reappears ∴ X⊤Xw= X⊤y set to 0 — the normal equations w⋆= (X⊤X)−1X⊤y if X⊤X is invertible
Read the third line again. At the optimum X⊤r = 0: the residual is orthogonal to every column of X. That single equation is the whole geometry of least squares, and it is the subject of the next slide.

Cost: forming X⊤X is O(nd2), inverting it O(d3). Fine for d ∼ 103; hopeless for the 109-parameter models in §8 — hence gradient descent.

The normal equations say X⊤(y − Xw) = 0, i.e. the residual is orthogonal to col(X). So:

ŷ = X(X⊤X)−1X⊤ y = Py
  • P is the orthogonal projector onto col(X): it satisfies P2 = P (projecting twice changes nothing) and P⊤ = P.
  • tr(P) = d+1 — the number of dimensions the model gets to "use up" fitting the data. This is exactly the degrees-of-freedom term in AIC and in the n−d−1 denominator of the noise-variance estimate.
  • Least squares is therefore not a statement about lines. It is a statement about the nearest point in a subspace, and it holds verbatim for any feature map.
Failure mode, visible in the picture. If two columns of X nearly coincide, the plane is spanned by near-parallel vectors: ŷ is still well defined, but w — the coordinates of ŷ in that basis — explodes. That is collinearity, and it is what ridge regression fixes.

X⊤X fails to be invertible whenever d+1 > n (more features than data) or when features are exactly collinear. Even when it is technically invertible, a tiny eigenvalue makes w⋆ wildly sensitive to noise in y.

Add an ℓ2 penalty on the weights:

Jλ(w) = ½‖Xw − y‖2 + λ2‖w‖2
∇Jλ= X⊤(Xw−y) + λw wλ⋆= (X⊤X + λI)−1X⊤y
Always invertible. Adding λI lifts every eigenvalue by λ: since X⊤X ⪰ 0, its eigenvalues are ≥ 0, so all become ≥ λ > 0. The problem is not merely solvable — it is well-conditioned.
What ridge does, in the SVD basis
X = UΣV⊤ ⇒ ŷ = ∑j σj2σj2 + λ (uj⊤y) uj

Each direction is shrunk by a factor between 0 and 1. Directions with large σj — where the data actually varies — pass through almost untouched. Directions with σj ≈ 0 — where the data says nothing — are crushed toward zero instead of being amplified by 1/σj.

ViewRidge is…
Numericalconditioning: bound the smallest eigenvalue away from 0
BayesianMAP under a Gaussian prior w ∼ 𝒩(0, σ2/λ · I)
Statisticala bias–variance trade: accept bias to cut variance
Deep learningweight decay — the same term, same gradient λw

Swapping ‖w‖22 for ‖w‖1 gives the lasso: no closed form, but sparse solutions. The general recipe — add a term that expresses what you believe about w — is the λ Ω(θ) from §1.2.

From scratch · normal equationstorch
import torch

def fit_closed_form(X, y, lam=0.0):
    """w = (X^T X + lam I)^-1 X^T y  -- the formula, literally.
    Never actually invert: solve the linear system instead."""
    n, d = X.shape
    A = X.T @ X + lam * torch.eye(d)      # (d, d)
    b = X.T @ y                           # (d,)
    return torch.linalg.solve(A, b)

def fit_qr(X, y):
    """What a real library does. Works even when X^T X is
    singular, and squares the condition number *once*
    instead of twice -- strictly more accurate."""
    return torch.linalg.lstsq(X, y).solution

# --- data: y = 3 x1 - 2 x2 + 1 + noise ----------------
torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.randn(200, 2)
X = torch.cat([torch.ones(200, 1), X], dim=1)   # bias column
w_true = torch.tensor([1.0, 3.0, -2.0])
y = X @ w_true + 0.1 * torch.randn(200)

print(fit_closed_form(X, y))   # tensor([1.002, 2.996, -1.993])
print(fit_qr(X, y))            # tensor([1.002, 2.996, -1.993])
Gradient descent · the version that scalestorch
def fit_gd(X, y, lr=0.05, steps=500, lam=0.0):
    """The only method that survives to section 8.
    Note grad = X^T r -- exactly the derivation on slide 12."""
    n, d = X.shape
    w = torch.zeros(d)
    for t in range(steps):
        r    = X @ w - y                  # residual   (n,)
        loss = 0.5 * (r @ r) / n
        grad = (X.T @ r) / n + lam * w    # (d,)
        w   -= lr * grad
    return w

print(fit_gd(X, y))            # tensor([1.002, 2.996, -1.993])
The point. The closed form exists only because the model is linear and the loss is quadratic. fit_gd never uses either fact — it only needs ∇J. That is why the same eight lines, with grad supplied by autograd, train every model in §3–§8.

Take the same linear score z = w⊤x + b — but z ∈ ℝ and we need a probability. Squash it:

p̂ = σ(z) = 11 + e−z ∈ (0, 1)

Why this function? Because it inverts the log-odds. If we model the log-odds as linear — the natural thing to do, since log-odds are unconstrained on ℝ — then σ is forced:

log p1 − p = z  ⇔  p = σ(z)

Useful identities

σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z),    σ′(z) = σ(z) (1 − σ(z))

The second one is the reason logistic regression is pleasant to differentiate — and, in §5, the reason deep sigmoid networks are unpleasant to train: σ′ ≤ ¼, always.

Likelihood

Model each label as Bernoulli with parameter p̂i = σ(zi). Written compactly for y ∈ {0,1}:

p(yi | xi) = p̂iyi (1 − p̂i)1−yi

Take −log of the product over the dataset. Products become sums; the maximiser is unchanged:

J(w) = −n∑i=1 [yi log p̂i + (1−yi) log(1−p̂i)]
Why not squared error? ½(σ(z) − y)2 is non-convex in w, and its gradient carries a factor σ′(z) that vanishes exactly when the model is confidently wrong — the worst possible time to stop learning. Cross-entropy has neither defect.

Gradient — chain rule, one link at a time

∂Ji∂p̂i = −yip̂i + 1−yi1−p̂i = p̂i − yip̂i(1−p̂i) ∂p̂i∂zi = p̂i(1 − p̂i) the sigmoid identity ∂Ji∂zi = p̂i − yi everything cancels ∇wJ= ∑i (p̂i − yi) xi = X⊤(p̂ − y)
Compare with slide 12. Linear regression gave ∇J = X⊤(ŷ − y). Logistic regression gives ∇J = X⊤(p̂ − y). Identical form.

This is not a coincidence. Both are generalised linear models with their canonical link, and for that whole family the gradient is always X⊤(prediction − target). Softmax + cross-entropy, next slide, is the same identity again — and it is why the backward pass of every classifier in §3–§8 starts with the single line dz = probs - onehot.

Now W ∈ ℝK×d produces K scores, called logits:

z = Wx + b ∈ ℝK
p̂k = softmax(z)k = ezk K∑j=1ezj
  • Shift invariance. softmax(z + c1) = softmax(z). Only differences of logits matter, so the parameterisation is over-complete by one degree of freedom — and subtracting maxk zk before exponentiating is free, which is how it is implemented safely.
  • It generalises the sigmoid. For K = 2, softmax reduces to σ(z1 − z2).
  • It is a soft arg-max, not a soft max: dividing the logits by a temperature T → 0 drives it to a one-hot vector.
The gradient, for the third time.
∂J∂z = p̂ − yone-hot,    ∂J∂W = (p̂ − y) x⊤
Softmax + cross-entropy, from scratchtorch
def softmax(z):
    """z: (B, K). Subtract the row max first -- exp(1000)
    overflows to inf, exp(0) does not. Mathematically a
    no-op by shift invariance."""
    z = z - z.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values
    e = z.exp()
    return e / e.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)

def cross_entropy(z, y):
    """z: (B, K) logits.  y: (B,) integer class ids.
    Uses log-sum-exp directly -- never log(softmax(z)),
    which loses precision when p is small."""
    z = z - z.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values
    logZ = z.exp().sum(-1).log()               # (B,)
    z_y  = z.gather(1, y[:, None]).squeeze(1)  # (B,)
    return (logZ - z_y).mean()

def backward(z, y):
    """dJ/dz = (p - onehot(y)) / B  -- the one line that
    every classifier in this lecture starts its backward
    pass with."""
    B, K = z.shape
    p = softmax(z)
    p[torch.arange(B), y] -= 1.0
    return p / B

nn.CrossEntropyLoss fuses all three of these and expects raw logits. Passing it softmax output is the most common bug in the course — it applies softmax twice, flattening the gradient.

Setting X⊤(σ(Xw) − y) = 0 gives a system that is transcendental in w — no algebraic solution exists. But J is still convex (∇2J = X⊤SX ⪰ 0 with S = diag(p̂i(1−p̂i))), so descent converges to the global optimum.

Gradient descent
wt+1 = wt − η ∇J(wt)
  • Batch GD uses all n points per step: exact gradient, O(nd) per step.
  • SGD uses one point (or a minibatch): a noisy but unbiased estimate, O(d) per step. Almost always wins, because n cheap noisy steps beat one expensive exact step.
  • Newton / IRLS uses the Hessian and converges in ~5 iterations — but costs O(d3) per step. Dead on arrival past §3.
One caveat. On separable data the MLE does not exist: scaling w → cw always lowers the loss, so ‖w‖ → ∞. Any λ > 0 of ridge penalty restores a finite optimum.
The wall. A linear model can only carve ℝd with a single hyperplane. XOR — four points, two classes — already defeats it. So does any dataset whose classes are nested, curved, or periodic.

Two ways out, and the whole history of the field is the argument between them:

  • Design the features by hand. Pick φ(x) yourself — SIFT, HOG, MFCC, n-grams — then run a linear model on top. Works, but needs a domain expert per problem, and the features never improve from data. (The kernel trick is this idea at its limit: an implicit, infinite φ — still fixed, and O(n2).)
  • Learn the features. Make φ itself parametric and fit it by the same gradient descent: f(x) = w⊤φθ(x) + b. That is precisely a neural network, and φθ is everything before the last layer.
The rest of the lecture. Keep the linear model — it is still the final layer, and the gradient X⊤(p̂−y) is still where the backward pass begins. Only now X is a learned representation.

Suppose we stack two linear layers, hoping depth alone adds power:

h= W1x + b1 ŷ= W2h + b2 = W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = (W2W1)call it W′ x + (W2b1 + b2)call it b′
Collapse. A composition of affine maps is an affine map. A 100-layer linear network has exactly the representational power of W′x + b′ — one layer — no matter how many parameters it has. The hypothesis class did not grow at all.

So insert a fixed, elementwise nonlinearity σ between the layers. It is the only thing standing between us and a very expensive linear model:

h = σ(W1x + b1),    ŷ = W2h + b2

Forward pass

h(0) = x
z(l) = W(l)h(l−1) + b(l) pre-activation
h(l) = σ(z(l)) elementwise, l = 1…L−1
ŷ = z(L) no σ on the output
Layer lShape of W(l)Params
1n1 × dn1(d+1)
2n2 × n1n2(n1+1)
LK × nL−1K(nL−1+1)
The one structural fact. Every weight is private: one number per (input unit, output unit) pair. Nothing is shared, so the network has no notion of an input being "near" another. §4 and §5 are both answers to that.
NameDefinitionDerivativeVerdict
sigmoid 1/(1+e−z) σ(1−σ) ≤ ¼ output layer only
tanh 2σ(2z) − 1 1 − tanh2 ≤ 1 ok inside gates (§6)
ReLU max(0, z) 1[z > 0] default for §3–§4
GELU z Φ(z) smooth, non-monotone default in §8
Why ReLU won. Its derivative is 1 on the active half, not ≤ ¼. Chain-ruling through L sigmoid layers multiplies at most (¼)L — at L = 10 that is 10−6, and the early layers never move. ReLU multiplies by 1.
Its failure mode. A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input has gradient exactly 0 forever — a "dead" unit. Leaky ReLU and GELU both fix this by never being exactly flat.
Theorem (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991)
Let σ be continuous and non-polynomial, and let f be continuous on a compact K ⊂ ℝd. Then for every ε > 0 there exist a width m and parameters such that
supx∈K |f(x) − m∑j=1 cj σ(wj⊤x + bj)| < ε

In words: a single hidden layer of sufficient width is dense in the continuous functions. The hypothesis class is, for practical purposes, everything.

Three things it does not say.
  • How large m must be. It can be exponential in d — the theorem is an existence result with no rate.
  • That gradient descent will find those parameters. It is about εapp only; §1.2's other two terms are untouched.
  • That the fit will generalise. Fitting the sample is not fitting the distribution.

Depth is what makes it practical: there are functions a depth-2 network needs O(2d) units to represent that a depth-d network represents with O(d). Width buys expressiveness; depth buys it cheaply.

Define the error signal at layer l — the sensitivity of the loss to that layer's pre-activation:

δ(l) ≡ ∂L∂z(l) ∈ ℝnl

Everything else follows from this one object. The four equations below are the complete algorithm; the rest of deep learning is bookkeeping around them.

The four equations of backprop
δ(L)= ∇ŷL = p̂ − y BP1 · base case, from §2 δ(l)= (W(l+1)⊤δ(l+1)) ⊙ σ′(z(l)) BP2 · the recursion ∂L/∂b(l)= δ(l) BP3 ∂L/∂W(l)= δ(l)h(l−1)⊤ BP4 · outer product
BP4 is the §2 gradient again. ∂L/∂W = δ · (input)⊤ is exactly X⊤(p̂−y) with X → h(l−1) and (p̂−y) → δ.

Where BP2 comes from

The loss depends on z(l) only through all of the next layer's pre-activations, so the multivariable chain rule sums over them:

δj(l)= ∑k ∂L∂zk(l+1) ∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l) zk(l+1)= ∑j Wkj(l+1) σ(zj(l)) + bk so the inner derivative is… ⇒ ∂zk(l+1)∂zj(l) = Wkj(l+1) σ′(zj(l)) δj(l)= σ′(zj(l)) ∑k Wkj(l+1)δk(l+1) = BP2, in components
Why it is cheap. A naive finite-difference gradient costs one forward pass per parameter: O(|θ|) passes. Backprop reuses δ(l+1) to build δ(l), so the whole gradient costs about two forward passes, total — independent of parameter count.

The memory cost is the catch: BP4 needs h(l−1), so every activation from the forward pass must be kept until the backward pass reaches it. That is why training memory scales with depth × batch × width, and why gradient checkpointing exists.

From scratch · forward + the four BP equationsHe init omitted
def forward(x, Ws, bs):
    """Cache every h -- BP4 needs them on the way back."""
    hs, zs = [x], []
    h = x
    for l, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(Ws, bs)):
        z = h @ W.T + b                     # (B, n_l)
        zs.append(z)
        h = z if l == len(Ws)-1 else z.clamp(min=0)   # ReLU
        hs.append(h)
    return hs, zs

def backward(hs, zs, y, Ws):
    """The four equations, applied right to left."""
    B = y.shape[0]
    p = zs[-1].softmax(-1)
    d = p.clone()
    d[torch.arange(B), y] -= 1.0
    d = d / B                               # BP1
    gW, gb = [None]*len(Ws), [None]*len(Ws)
    for l in reversed(range(len(Ws))):
        gW[l] = d.T @ hs[l]                 # BP4
        gb[l] = d.sum(0)                    # BP3
        if l > 0:
            d = (d @ Ws[l]) * (zs[l-1] > 0) # BP2
    return gW, gb
The same model in PyTorchtorch.nn
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),               # logits: no softmax here
)
The training loop — unchanged for the rest of the lecturetorch
opt   = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4,
                          weight_decay=0.01)  # <- ridge, from §2
lossf = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for xb, yb in loader:
    loss = lossf(model(xb), yb)   # forward; BP1 lives in here
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()               # BP2-BP4, automatically
    opt.step()                    # w <- w - lr * grad
Read the loop once, carefully. Nothing in it mentions MLPs. Swap model for a CNN, an LSTM or a Transformer and not one line changes. That is the payoff of §1's framing: architecture and optimisation are genuinely separable concerns.

Feed a 224×224×3 image to a fully connected layer with 1000 hidden units:

224 × 224 × 3 × 1000 ≈ 1.5 × 108 weights in the first layer alone
  • Statistically hopeless. More parameters in one layer than ImageNet has pixels of training signal per class. εest dominates.
  • It throws away the grid. The MLP sees a flat vector: permute all pixels with a fixed random permutation and re-train, and it learns exactly as well. That tells you it never used the fact that neighbouring pixels are related.
  • No translation equivariance. A cat learned in the top-left corner is, to this model, unrelated to the same cat in the bottom-right. Every position must be learned separately.
The fix, in one sentence. Stop giving every (input, output) pair its own weight. Tie them: use the same small set of weights at every spatial position. That is a convolution, and it is §4.

For a 1-D signal x and kernel w of size k:

yi = k−1∑a=0 wa xi+a + b

and in 2-D, with kernel k×k:

Yi,j = k−1∑a=0 k−1∑b=0 Wa,b Xi+a, j+b + b
Pedantic note. This is strictly cross-correlation; true convolution flips the kernel (xi−a). Since W is learned, the flip is absorbed into the learned values and the distinction is irrelevant in practice. Every framework calls this "conv".
Still a linear layer — just a constrained one
y = Tx,   T = w₀w₁w₂00 0w₀w₁w₂0 00w₀w₁w₂

A Toeplitz matrix: banded (sparsity = locality) and constant along each diagonal (tying = translation equivariance). Backprop needs no new theory — §3's four equations apply verbatim to T.

Output size — the formula to memorise
Hout = ⌊ Hin + 2p − d(k−1) − 1s ⌋ + 1
KnobEffectCommon choice
padding p adds a border of zeros; preserves size and stops the map shrinking every layer p = (k−1)/2 → "same"
stride s step between windows; s=2 halves the map — downsampling with learned weights 1, or 2 to downsample
dilation d spaces the kernel taps out; grows the receptive field without more parameters or lost resolution 1; >1 for segmentation, audio
Sanity check. k=3, p=1, s=1, d=1 gives Hout = Hin. That is the default building block of essentially every modern vision network, stacked dozens deep.

Real inputs have channels: RGB, or the Cin feature maps produced by the previous layer. A kernel is therefore a volume Cin×k×k, and there are Cout of them:

Yo,i,j = Cin∑c=1 k∑a k∑b Wo,c,a,b Xc, i+a, j+b + bo
TensorShape
input X (B, Cin, H, W)
weight W (Cout, Cin, k, k)
bias b (Cout,)
output Y (B, Cout, H′, W′)
Parameter count. Cout × Cin × k2 + Cout — note that H and W do not appear. A conv layer has the same size for a 32×32 thumbnail and a 4K frame. That is what weight tying bought.
Two 3×3 beats one 5×5. Same receptive field, but 18 weights instead of 25 and two nonlinearities instead of one. This is the whole design of VGG, and 3×3 has been the default ever since.

Pooling

Yi,j = maxa,b∈window X2i+a, 2j+b
  • No parameters. A fixed reduction, so it costs nothing statistically.
  • Downsamples by 2×, doubling the receptive field of everything above — turning the linear growth above into geometric growth.
  • Buys local invariance: shifting the input by one pixel usually leaves the max unchanged.
Equivariance vs invariance. Convolution is equivariant — f(Tvx) = Tvf(x); pooling converts that into invariance, f(Tvx) = f(x). Want equivariance in the middle, invariance only at the end — discard position too early and you cannot localise anything.

Modern nets often drop pooling for stride-2 convolutions (learned downsampling), and replace the final flatten with global average pooling so the network accepts any input size.

From scratch · explicit, then vectorisedtorch
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def conv2d_naive(X, W, b, stride=1, pad=0):
    """X: (B,Cin,H,Wd)  W: (Cout,Cin,k,k)  -- the formula
    transcribed literally. Correct, and far too slow."""
    X = F.pad(X, (pad,)*4)
    B, Cin, H, Wd = X.shape
    Cout, _, k, _ = W.shape
    Ho = (H - k)//stride + 1
    Wo = (Wd - k)//stride + 1
    Y = torch.zeros(B, Cout, Ho, Wo)
    for o in range(Cout):
        for i in range(Ho):
            for j in range(Wo):
                patch = X[:, :, i*stride:i*stride+k,
                                j*stride:j*stride+k]
                Y[:, o, i, j] = (patch * W[o]).sum((1,2,3)) + b[o]
    return Y

def conv2d_im2col(X, W, b, stride=1, pad=0):
    """What cuDNN does: unfold every patch into a column,
    then the whole convolution is ONE matrix multiply --
    which is exactly the Toeplitz view from slide 30."""
    B, Cin, H, Wd = X.shape
    Cout, _, k, _ = W.shape
    cols = F.unfold(X, k, stride=stride, padding=pad)  # (B, Cin*k*k, L)
    out  = W.view(Cout, -1) @ cols + b[:, None]        # (B, Cout, L)
    Ho = (H + 2*pad - k)//stride + 1
    return out.view(B, Cout, Ho, -1)
A small CNN, and the residual blocktorch.nn
class Block(nn.Module):
    """conv -> norm -> act, twice, plus a skip.
    The skip is what lets this stack 100 layers deep:
    dL/dx = dL/dy * (1 + dF/dx), so the gradient has a
    path with derivative 1 -- compare BP2 in section 3."""
    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.f = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, stride, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, 1, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out),
        )
        self.skip = (nn.Identity() if stride == 1 and c_in == c_out
                     else nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 1, stride, bias=False))

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.relu(self.f(x) + self.skip(x))

net = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    Block(64, 64), Block(64, 128, stride=2),
    Block(128, 256, stride=2),
    nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),      # -> (B, 256, 1, 1), any input size
    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(256, 10),   # the section-2 linear model
)

The last two lines. Global average pooling, then nn.Linear: after all of that, we are still fitting a §2 linear classifier — just on features the network learned for itself.

Everything so far assumed x ∈ ℝd with d fixed and known. A sentence, a waveform, a stock series and a video all violate that.

Naive fixWhy it fails
Pad / truncate to a fixed T, feed an MLP weights at position 7 are unrelated to those at position 8, so nothing transfers between positions; and T is a hard ceiling
Bag of words: average the tokens order is destroyed — "dog bites man" = "man bites dog"
1-D convolution genuinely good, and used in practice — but the receptive field grows only linearly with depth, so long-range dependencies need very deep stacks
What we actually want. One set of weights that processes a step, applied at every step, plus a state that carries information forward. Weight tying along the time axis — precisely the §4 move, with "position in the image" replaced by "position in the sequence".

The consequences mirror §4 exactly: parameter count independent of T, and equivariance — now to time shifts rather than spatial ones.

The recurrence

ht = tanh( Whhht−1 + Wxhxt + bh)
ŷt = Whyht + by
The subscript that matters. Whh, Wxh, Why carry no t. The same three matrices are used at every step — so the parameter count is independent of sequence length, and a network trained on length-50 sequences can be run on length-500.
  • ht is a lossy summary of x1..t, compressed into a fixed-size vector regardless of how much history there is.
  • Unrolled, an RNN is a very deep MLP — depth T — whose layers happen to share weights. Nothing new is needed to train it.
  • Computation is inherently sequential: ht needs ht−1. No parallelism over time — the defect §8 exists to remove.

Unrolled, the loss at step T depends on Whh through every step, so the gradient sums over all of them (this is BPTT):

∂LT∂Whh = T∑t=1 ∂LT∂hT ∂hT∂ht ∂ht∂Whh

The middle factor is the problem. It telescopes into a product:

∂hT∂ht = T∏k=t+1 Whh⊤ diag(tanh′(zk))
A product of T−t matrices. Take norms: with γ = ‖Whh‖ and tanh′ ≤ 1,
‖∂hT/∂ht‖ ≤ γT−t
γ < 1 ⇒ vanishing — the gradient from step T reaches step t multiplied by γT−t ≈ 0. γ > 1 ⇒ exploding — it arrives as ∞, and NaN follows.

Precisely: if the largest singular value of Whh is < 1/max tanh′ = 1, vanishing is guaranteed. There is no learning rate that fixes it, because the signal itself is gone — not merely small.

Partial remedies
Exploding is easy: clip the global gradient norm (clip_grad_norm_) — the direction is right, only the length is absurd.
Vanishing is hard: nothing survives to rescale. It needs an architectural fix, which is §6.
From scratch · the cell and the unrolled looptorch
class RNNCell(nn.Module):
    """One step. Note there is no time index on any weight:
    this single object is called T times per sequence."""
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_h):
        super().__init__()
        self.Wx = nn.Linear(d_in, d_h, bias=False)
        self.Wh = nn.Linear(d_h,  d_h, bias=True)

    def forward(self, x_t, h):                 # x_t (B,d_in), h (B,d_h)
        return torch.tanh(self.Wx(x_t) + self.Wh(h))

class RNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_h, d_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.cell = RNNCell(d_in, d_h)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d_h, d_out)
        self.d_h  = d_h

    def forward(self, x):                      # x (B, T, d_in)
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        h  = x.new_zeros(B, self.d_h)
        ys = []
        for t in range(T):                     # <- strictly sequential
            h = self.cell(x[:, t], h)          # the whole recurrence
            ys.append(self.head(h))
        return torch.stack(ys, dim=1), h       # (B,T,d_out), (B,d_h)
The library version, and trainingtorch.nn
rnn = nn.RNN(d_in, d_h, num_layers=2,
             batch_first=True, nonlinearity='tanh')
y, h_T = rnn(x)        # y (B,T,d_h) -- the loop, fused in C++

for xb, yb in loader:
    logits, _ = model(xb)
    loss = lossf(logits.reshape(-1, K), yb.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()                     # BPTT: unrolls T deep

    # 1. exploding gradients are the norm, not the exception
    nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
    opt.step()

# 2. streams longer than memory: truncated BPTT -- carry h
#    forward but cut the graph, so backward stops here
h = h.detach()
Two lines that are not optional. clip_grad_norm_ and h.detach() are what make RNN training terminate at all. Forget detach and the graph grows without bound until memory runs out.

Notice for t in range(T): T sequential kernel launches a GPU cannot overlap. §8 replaces that loop with one matrix multiply.

The RNN's fault is structural: every path from ht to hT passes through T−t multiplications by Whh and tanh′.

The fix. Add a second state — the cell state ct — whose update is additive, not multiplicative:
ct = ct−1 + (something)

Then ∂ct/∂ct−1 = I, and the gradient travels backward along the cell state unchanged, for any number of steps. That highway is the constant error carousel.

But a state that only ever accumulates saturates and can never forget. So gate it — multiply the two terms by learned, input-dependent values in (0,1):

ct = ft ⊙ ct−1how much to keep + it ⊙ c̃thow much to write

Now ∂ct/∂ct−1 = diag(ft). The network chooses the decay rate per dimension, per timestep. Set ft ≈ 1 and the memory is preserved perfectly; set it near 0 and it is cleared on purpose.

All six equations
ft= σ(Wf[ht−1, xt] + bf) forget it= σ(Wi[ht−1, xt] + bi) input ot= σ(Wo[ht−1, xt] + bo) output c̃t= tanh(Wc[ht−1, xt] + bc) candidate ct= ft ⊙ ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t the highway ht= ot ⊙ tanh(ct) what the rest of the net sees
GateQuestion it answers
f forgetwhat should I erase from memory?
i inputwhat of the new candidate is worth storing?
o outputwhat of memory is relevant right now?

All three gates read the same [ht−1, xt], so in practice one matrix of shape 4d × (d+din) computes all four pre-activations in a single GEMM, then splits. Parameters: 4d(d + din + 1) — four times a vanilla RNN.

Differentiate the cell-state update:

∂ct∂ct−1 = diag(ft)  ⇒  ∂cT∂ct = T∏k=t+1 diag(fk)
Compare with §5. The RNN's product was over Whh⊤diag(tanh′) — fixed, and unadaptable per step. The LSTM's is over gates the network computes: if remembering matters, descent learns f ≈ 1 and the product becomes I.
Initialise the forget bias to 1. At bf = 0, f ≈ 0.5 and memory halves every step. Setting bf = 1 starts the cell in "remember by default" mode — free accuracy.
StatesGatesParams
RNNh— d(d+din)
LSTMh, cf, i, o 4×
GRUhreset, update 3×

The GRU merges c into h and ties i = 1 − f. It keeps the additive path, costs 25% less, and performs comparably — pick either.

LSTM cell from scratch · one fused GEMMtorch
class LSTMCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_h):
        super().__init__()
        # one matrix for all four pre-activations, then split
        self.W = nn.Linear(d_in + d_h, 4 * d_h)
        self.d_h = d_h
        # remember-by-default: forget bias = 1
        nn.init.zeros_(self.W.bias)
        nn.init.ones_(self.W.bias[:d_h])

    def forward(self, x_t, state):
        h, c = state
        z = self.W(torch.cat([x_t, h], dim=-1))     # (B, 4*d_h)
        f, i, g, o = z.chunk(4, dim=-1)

        f, i, o = f.sigmoid(), i.sigmoid(), o.sigmoid()
        g = torch.tanh(g)                       # candidate

        c = f * c + i * g          # <- the additive highway
        h = o * torch.tanh(c)
        return h, (h, c)

# library version, cuDNN-fused over the whole sequence.
# bidirectional = a second pass right-to-left, concatenated:
# fine when the sequence is fully known (tagging), forbidden
# when generating -- it would read the future.
lstm = nn.LSTM(d_in, d_h, num_layers=2, batch_first=True,
               bidirectional=True, dropout=0.1)
y, (h_T, c_T) = lstm(x)              # y: (B, T, 2*d_h)
The question. At decoder step i, which parts of the source are relevant right now? That is content-dependent, so it cannot be fixed at design time — it must be computed, and learned.
The mechanism. Score every source position against the current query, normalise the scores into weights that sum to 1, and return the weighted average of the source vectors. Differentiable end to end.
The vocabulary. It is a soft dictionary lookup: a query is matched against keys to produce weights, which retrieve a blend of values — instead of one exact hit.
Hard dictionaryAttention
key you look upq — the query: what I am looking for
keys in the tablekj — the keys: what each position advertises
stored entriesvj — the values: what each position returns
exact match, one hitsimilarity score, all hits, weighted

The three steps

ej= q⊤kj / √dk 1. score every position αj= softmaxj(e) 2. normalise: α ≥ 0, ∑α = 1 out= ∑j αjvj 3. retrieve the blend
All of it at once, for all queries
Attn(Q, K, V) = softmax( QK⊤√dk )V

Shapes: Q ∈ ℝn×dk, K ∈ ℝm×dk, V ∈ ℝm×dv; the softmax is row-wise over m; the output is n×dv. Two matrix multiplies and a softmax — every position handled in parallel.

In self-attention the same sequence X ∈ ℝn×d supplies all three, through three learned projections:

Q = XWQ,   K = XWK,   V = XWV

Those three matrices are the only parameters in an attention layer — and, as in §4 and §5, they carry no position index: the same projections are applied at every token. Weight tying again, now along the sequence axis.

Why divide by √dk?
If the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then
q⊤k = dk∑i=1 qiki  ⇒  Var = dk,   sd = √dk
With dk = 64 the scores have spread ±8. Softmax of scores that far apart is essentially a one-hot vector — and there the softmax Jacobian is zero, so no gradient flows. Dividing by √dk restores unit variance and keeps the softmax in its responsive range.
Complexity, honestly. QK⊤ is n×n: O(n2d) time and memory. That quadratic term is the price of the O(1) path length, and the reason context length is the central engineering problem in modern LLMs.

A single softmax produces one weighting. But a token may need syntax from one place and semantics from another. So split the model dimension into h heads of width dk = d/h and attend independently in each:

headi = Attn(XWiQ, XWiK, XWiV)
MHA(X) = [head1; …; headh] WO
It is free. Because dk = d/h, total parameters and FLOPs are the same as one head of full width. Heads are a reshape, not extra capacity — (B,n,d) → (B,h,n,d/h) — and the batched matmul handles them all at once.
Masking. To stop a position seeing the future (needed whenever the model generates), add −∞ to the scores above the diagonal before the softmax; those weights become exactly 0. The same trick with a padding mask ignores padded positions. One line, and it is the difference between an encoder and a decoder.

In production use F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True): same maths, but fused and never materialising the n×n matrix, which is what makes long contexts affordable.

Multi-head self-attention from scratchtorch
class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, causal=False):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.h  = n_heads
        self.dk = d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv  = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)  # fused Q,K,V
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)      # W^O
        self.causal = causal

    def forward(self, x):                       # x: (B, n, d)
        B, n, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)

        # (B,n,d) -> (B,h,n,dk): heads are just a reshape
        split = lambda t: t.view(B, n, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2)
        q, k, v = map(split, (q, k, v))

        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / self.dk ** 0.5   # (B,h,n,n)
        if self.causal:                    # no peeking at the future
            m = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool,
                           device=x.device).triu(1)
            att = att.masked_fill(m, float('-inf'))

        att = att.softmax(dim=-1)
        out = att @ v                                 # (B, h, n, dk)
        out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, n, d)    # merge heads
        return self.proj(out)
The two sublayers do different jobs
Attention is the only place tokens interact. It is a weighted average — a linear operation given the weights — so on its own it could not compute much.

FFN is where the nonlinear work happens, applied independently to each position. It is a §3 MLP, width 4d, and it holds roughly two-thirds of the parameters of a Transformer.
Residuals are load-bearing. x ← x + F(x) gives ∂xout/∂xin = I + ∂F/∂x. That I is the same constant-error-carousel trick as §6's cell state — the reason 100-layer stacks train at all.
Pre-LN vs post-LN. The 2017 paper put LayerNorm after the addition; that needs a learning-rate warmup to be stable. Putting it before the sublayer (pre-LN, drawn here) trains without warmup and is what essentially every model since ~2020 uses.
SublayerParamsCost
attention4d2 O(n2d + nd2)
FFN8d2 O(nd2)
The gap. Permute the rows of X and every row of Attn(X) is permuted the same way and otherwise unchanged. Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: it sees a set, not a sequence. Order must be supplied explicitly.

Sinusoidal encoding (Vaswani et al.)

PE(p, 2i) = sin( p100002i/d)
PE(p, 2i+1) = cos( p100002i/d)
  • Every position gets a unique code, built from wavelengths spanning 2π to 10000·2π — a binary-counter pattern in continuous form.
  • Relative offsets are linear. PEp+k is a fixed rotation of PEp, so "3 tokens back" is a relationship the attention scores can learn to detect.
  • It extrapolates to lengths never seen in training, because it is a formula rather than a lookup table.

Alternatives: learned absolute embeddings (simple, but capped at the trained length); RoPE, which rotates q and k by a position-dependent angle so that q⊤k depends only on the relative offset — now the standard in large language models.

One blocktorch
class Block(nn.Module):
    """Pre-LN: x + Attn(LN(x)), then x + FFN(LN(x))."""
    def __init__(self, d, h, p=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1  = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d, h, causal=True)
        self.ln2  = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.ffn  = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(4 * d, d), nn.Dropout(p),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # mix ACROSS tokens
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))    # think PER token
        return x
Training — the same loop as slide 28torch
for idx, targets in loader:          # next-token prediction
    logits = model(idx)                          # (B, n, V)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),
                           targets.view(-1))     # section 2!
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()                              # section 3!
    nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step()
The stacktorch
class Transformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab, d=512, h=8, n_layers=6,
                 max_len=1024):
        super().__init__()
        self.tok = nn.Embedding(vocab, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(max_len, d)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            Block(d, h) for _ in range(n_layers))
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d, vocab, bias=False)
        self.head.weight = self.tok.weight     # weight tying

    def forward(self, idx):                    # idx: (B, n)
        pos = torch.arange(idx.shape[1], device=idx.device)
        x = self.tok(idx) + self.pos(pos)      # (B, n, d)
        for blk in self.blocks:                # over DEPTH,
            x = blk(x)                         # not over time
        return self.head(self.ln_f(x))         # (B, n, vocab)
Every section is visible in these two panels. §1 the loss is cross-entropy on a simplex · §2 self.head is a linear model with gradient (p̂−y) · §3 the FFN is an MLP and .backward() is BP1–BP4 · §4/§5 weight tying — one block serves every position, as a kernel served every pixel · §6 the residual x + … is the constant error carousel · §7 attention, the one new operation.
Model Inductive bias What is tied Path length Parallel over Cost / layer Breaks on
Linear the target is an affine function of the given features nothing to tie 1 everything O(nd) anything curved — XOR
MLP none — the input is an unstructured vector nothing to tie 1 everything O(d2) high-dimensional structured input: too many parameters
CNN locality + translation equivariance kernel, across space O(n/k) by depth all positions O(nkd2) long-range and non-local dependencies
RNN causal order; a Markov summary suffices cell, across time O(n) batch only O(nd2) vanishing gradients past ~10 steps
LSTM as RNN, plus: memory should persist by default cell, across time O(n), but additive batch only O(nd2) the sequential loop — cannot be parallelised
Attention relevance is content-dependent, not positional Q/K/V projections, across positions 1 all positions O(n2d) quadratic memory in context length
Transformer attention + explicit position + per-token MLP the whole block, across positions 1 all positions and batch O(n2d + nd2) context length; data hunger (weak prior)

The pattern. Reading down, the inductive bias gets weaker and the path length gets shorter. Weaker priors need more data; shorter paths let gradients survive.

Choosing one. Small data with real structure → take the strong prior. Large data with long-range structure → the Transformer, because it can learn the prior a CNN was handed.

Nothing was discarded. A Transformer still ends in the §2 linear classifier, still trains by §3 backprop, still borrows §6's residual path. Only the middle box changed.

Carried over. Colour is never decoration: every box, arrow and symbol is tinted by what kind of quantity it is. Part I needed four kinds. Part II needs a fifth.
data Activations computed forward. x, h(l)
params What the optimiser is allowed to change. W, β, γ
loss The scalar objective. L(θ)
grads Anything travelling backward. gt = ∇L
state New. Memory the optimiser (or a norm layer) carries between steps — neither parameter nor gradient.  mt, vt, μrun

It earns its own colour because it is the thing you pay for: state is the reason Adam costs 3× the memory of plain SGD, and the reason a BatchNorm model behaves differently in train() and eval().

Part I built fθ. Training means solving

θ⋆ = arg minθ∈ℝP  L(θ),   L(θ) = 1n n∑i=1 ℓ(fθ(xi), yi)

Four facts about this problem decide everything that follows.

  • It is non-convex in θ as soon as there are two layers. No closed form, no certificate of optimality, no uniqueness — even the permutation symmetry of a hidden layer gives d! copies of every minimum.
  • It is enormous. P is 108–1012. Anything costing O(P2) memory — a Hessian, a covariance, a full preconditioner — is not merely slow, it is unstorable.
  • One thing is cheap. Reverse-mode AD gives the entire gradient ∇L ∈ ℝP for about 2× the cost of one forward pass — independent of P. That asymmetry is why first-order methods won.
  • We do not want L small. We want the risk R(θ) = 𝔼p[ℓ] small. So the optimiser is not allowed to be too good: how we reach a minimum changes which minimum we reach.

The only oracle we have

θ ↦ (L(θ), ∇L(θ)) cost ≈ 3 forward passes, memory O(P)
Method classUsesMemoryViable?
Grid / random searchL only×1no — curse of dim.
Zeroth-order / ESL only×1only if P tiny
First-order∇L×1–3yes — §10–§11
Structured 2nd-order∇L + shape×2–4yes — §12
Full Newton∇2L×Pnever
The frame for §10–§12. Given only (L, ∇L) at one point per step, and O(P) memory, produce the best possible step. That is the entire design space, and it is smaller than it looks.

Near any point, L looks quadratic. Diagonalise the Hessian H = QΛQ⊤: in eigen-coordinates the problem decouples into P independent 1-D problems, one per eigenvalue λi, and gradient descent contracts each one at its own rate.

zi(t) = (1 − ηλi)t zi(0) stable iff η < 2/λmax
θt+1 = θt − η Pt gt where gt = ∇Lℬt(θt) on minibatch ℬt

The gradient says which way is downhill in the current coordinates. Pt says how much to trust each coordinate. Choosing P is choosing an optimiser.

MethodPtState / param§

SGD + momentumI, on a smoothed g13

RMSPropdiag(1/√EMA[g2])13
Adam / AdamWdiag(1/√v̂), on smoothed g23
Shampoo / SOAPL−1/4⊗R−1/4 (Kronecker)2–44
Muonwhitens the momentum matrix: UV⊤14
NewtonH−1P—

Read the table as a ladder of how much structure you admit: nothing (I) → per-coordinate (diagonal) → per-matrix (Kronecker / spectral) → everything (Newton, unaffordable). Every rung buys better conditioning and costs memory.

Why P is not optional. ∇L is a covector: it lives in the dual space. Adding it to θ is a type error that only a choice of metric repairs, and P = I is the arbitrary choice that “all parameters are measured in the same units.” They are not.
Sanity check. Rescale one layer's weights by 103 and rescale its output by 10−3. The function is unchanged, the loss is unchanged — but plain SGD now takes completely different steps. Any method whose behaviour survives this test (Adam, Muon, normalised nets) is doing something right.
The loop · annotatedtorch
model = MyNet()                       # §13 decides the numbers inside
opt   = torch.optim.AdamW(            # §11 decides P
            model.parameters(),
            lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95),
            weight_decay=0.1)
sched = warmup_cosine(opt, warmup=2000, total=100_000)

for step, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):        # §10: minibatch
    loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y)       #   forward
    loss.backward()                           #   -> p.grad for every p

    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(           # §11: rare-event insurance
        model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

    opt.step()                                #   theta <- theta - eta P g
    sched.step()                              #   eta <- eta(t)
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)           #   grads do NOT reset themselves
Order matters. clip before step; zero_grad after. Forgetting the last line silently accumulates gradients across steps — which is exactly how gradient accumulation is implemented on purpose, and the most common bug when it is not.
L(θ + Δ)≈ L(θ) + g⊤Δ first-order Taylor — all we can afford Δ⋆= arg min‖Δ‖2 ≤ r g⊤Δ unbounded without the constraint = −r g‖g‖2 Cauchy–Schwarz, equality at antiparallel ∴ θt+1= θt − η gt absorb r/‖g‖ into η
Read line 2 carefully. The norm in the constraint is a modelling choice, not a law. Choose ‖·‖2 and you get gradient descent. Choose a weighted norm and you get a preconditioner. Choose the spectral norm on a weight matrix and you get Muon (§12). Same three lines, different geometry.
And the ceiling. If L is β-smooth, then η ≤ 1/β guarantees L decreases every step, by at least (η/2)‖g‖2. Past 2/β it provably diverges. There is no learning rate that is “aggressive but safe” — there is a number, and it is 1/λmax.

The exact gradient costs n backward passes:

∇L(θ) = 1n n∑i=1 ∇ℓi(θ) an average of n vectors

Spending n = 109 gradient evaluations to compute one number to 8 digits, and then taking a step whose direction is only trustworthy for a few units of distance, is a bad trade. Sample instead:

gt = 1B ∑i∈ℬt ∇ℓi(θt),    𝔼[gt] = ∇L(θt)
  • Unbiased for any B, including B = 1. Sampling with replacement makes this exact; the epoch-shuffling everyone actually uses is slightly biased within an epoch and slightly better in practice.
  • Variance 𝔼‖gt − ∇L‖2 = σ2/B — noise falls as 1/√B, cost rises as B. Diminishing returns are built in.
  • Cost per unit progress is what matters, and it is minimised at B ≪ n. Full batch is the worst point on the curve.
Per stepFull batchMinibatch B=1024
Gradient evals10⁹1024
Wall-clockhours< 1 s
Steps per epoch110⁶
Gradient error0σ/32
Loss reached in 1 epochbarely movedconverged
Robbins–Monro (1951). Stochastic approximation converges for a decaying step size satisfying ∑ηt = ∞ (you can still travel any distance) and ∑ηt2 < ∞ (the accumulated noise is finite). ηt ∝ 1/t qualifies; a constant η does not — which is exactly why every real run ends with a decay schedule (§11.9).
The modern reading. We are not doing stochastic approximation of a fixed target. We are doing single-pass optimisation of a loss we will never see twice, where n is effectively infinite. Then noise is not an error to be averaged away — it is the price of seeing new data, and it is a bargain.

With constant η, the iterates stop improving once the drift toward the minimum balances the diffusion from gradient noise. On a quadratic with curvature λ and noise σ2, the stationary spread is

𝔼‖θ∞ − θ⋆‖2  ≈  ησ22λB
  • Halving η halves the squared radius. This is the whole mechanism behind the staircase in every published loss curve: each drop in η shrinks the ball, and the loss immediately falls to the new floor.
  • Doubling B does the same thing — at twice the cost. η is free; B is not.
  • The ratio η/B (“temperature”) is the single knob that sets the noise level. Two runs with the same η/B behave remarkably alike — the origin of the linear scaling rule on the next slide.
Do not over-read the formula. It is derived on a quadratic with isotropic noise. In a real network the noise covariance is anisotropic and aligned with the Hessian, which is why SGD noise pushes toward flat directions rather than diffusing uniformly (§10.6).
  • Linear scaling rule. Multiply B by k → multiply η by k, to hold the temperature η/B fixed. Verified up to B = 8k on ImageNet; needs a warmup to survive the first few hundred steps. For Adam the analogous rule is closer to η ∝ √B.
  • Critical batch size Bcrit. Steps needed obey S ≈ Smin(1 + Bcrit/B) and examples needed E ≈ Emin(1 + B/Bcrit). Below Bcrit you are wasting time; above it you are wasting compute. Bcrit grows during training as the gradient noise scale grows.
  • Gradient accumulation gives you any B regardless of memory: run k micro-batches, sum the grads, step once. Mathematically identical to a big batch — except for BatchNorm, whose statistics are per-micro-batch (§14.3).
Practical reading. Pick the largest B that keeps the accelerators busy and stays at or below Bcrit; then tune η. Never tune B to improve the loss — you are tuning η/B by accident.
From scratch · SGD with momentum + decaytorch
class SGD:
    """Minimal but faithful: this is PyTorch's SGD,
    including its (non-standard) momentum convention."""

    def __init__(self, params, lr, momentum=0.0,
                 weight_decay=0.0, nesterov=False):
        self.p  = list(params)
        self.lr, self.mu = lr, momentum
        self.wd, self.nesterov = weight_decay, nesterov
        self.buf = [None] * len(self.p)          # <- the state

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self):
        for i, p in enumerate(self.p):
            if p.grad is None: continue
            g = p.grad
            if self.wd: g = g + self.wd * p      # L2 -> INTO the gradient
            if self.mu:
                b = self.buf[i]
                if b is None:
                    b = self.buf[i] = g.clone()  # first step: b = g
                else:
                    b.mul_(self.mu).add_(g)      # b <- mu*b + g
                g = g + self.mu * b if self.nesterov else b
            p.add_(g, alpha=-self.lr)            # theta <- theta - lr*g

    def zero_grad(self):
        for p in self.p: p.grad = None
The library calltorch.optim
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1,
                      momentum=0.9, weight_decay=5e-4,
                      nesterov=True)
# classic ResNet/ImageNet recipe: lr 0.1 per 256 examples,
# cosine or step decay, 5-epoch linear warmup.
Footgun 1 · the momentum convention. PyTorch uses b ← μb + g, then steps by −ηb. The textbook (and TensorFlow's use_nesterov=False) uses b ← μb + (1−μ)g. The two differ by a factor of 1/(1−μ) = 10 at μ = 0.9. Porting a learning rate between frameworks without checking this is a classic silent 10× error.
Footgun 2 · weight_decay is L2 here. Notice the line g = g + wd * p: the decay is folded into the gradient, so momentum smooths it and (in Adam) the second moment rescales it. For SGD that is harmless and equivalent to adding ½λ‖θ‖2 to the loss. For Adam it is not — see §11.8.
Also. zero_grad(set_to_none=True) is the default since 2.0: it frees the gradient buffers instead of filling them with zeros, saving one full parameter-sized tensor of memory and one kernel launch per parameter.
vt = β vt−1 + gt,    θt+1 = θt − η vt  ≡  vt = t∑k=0 βkgt−k

An exponentially weighted sum with effective window 1/(1−β): 10 steps at β = 0.9, 100 at 0.99. The only state is one buffer the size of the parameters.

  • Along the valley the gradient keeps its sign, so the sum is geometric: v → g/(1−β). The effective step is 10× larger than η at β = 0.9 — without ever raising η past the stability limit.
  • Across the valley the gradient alternates sign, so consecutive terms cancel and the oscillation is damped instead of amplified.
  • It is genuinely accelerated. On a quadratic, the optimal β = ((√κ−1)/(√κ+1))2 gives convergence in O(√κ) steps rather than O(κ). For κ = 104 that is 100 steps instead of 10 000.
  • It also averages away minibatch noise for free: the buffer is a 1/(1−β)-sample mean, so momentum with B behaves a little like SGD with a larger batch.
Nesterov, in one line. Evaluate the gradient after the momentum carry, at θt − ηβvt−1, not at θt. You feel the wall before you hit it, so overshoot is corrected one step earlier. Deterministically it improves the constant; stochastically the gain is small but it costs nothing — nesterov=True.

AdaGrad · Duchi et al. 2011

vt,i = t∑s=1 gs,i2,   θt+1,i = θt,i − η√vt,i + ε gt,i
  • The idea, and it is a good one. A coordinate whose gradient has been large has already moved a lot — slow it down. A coordinate that has barely been touched (a rare word's embedding, a rarely-active feature) gets a large step. This is why AdaGrad was a breakthrough for sparse convex problems.
  • The flaw. v is a sum, so it is monotonically increasing. The effective learning rate decays like 1/√t forever, whether or not the problem calls for it. On a deep net it grinds to a halt long before convergence.

RMSProp · Hinton, lecture slide, 2012

vt = β2vt−1 + (1−β2)gt2 a running average, not a sum

One symbol changed, and the denominator now tracks the current gradient scale instead of the whole history. √vt is simply an online estimate of the RMS of that coordinate's gradient, so the update is ≈ ±η in every coordinate.

Nothing is free. Dividing by √v makes the update magnitude independent of the gradient magnitude. That is exactly the property we want for conditioning — and exactly the property that breaks weight decay (§11.6) and makes early training fragile before v is a good estimate (§11.7, warmup).
for t = 1, 2, …
  gt = ∇Lℬt(θt−1)
  mt = β1mt−1 + (1−β1)gt 1st moment — direction
  vt = β2vt−1 + (1−β2)gt2 2nd moment — scale
  m̂t = mt/(1−β1t) bias correction
  v̂t = vt/(1−β2t)
  θt = θt−1 − η m̂t ∕ (√v̂t + ε) elementwise

Why bias correction is not optional

mt= (1−β1)t∑s=1β1t−sgs unroll from m0 = 0 𝔼[mt]= (1 − β1t) 𝔼[g] if 𝔼[gs] is roughly constant m1= 0.1 g1 at β1=0.9 — a 10× underestimate v1= 0.001 g12 at β2=0.999 — a 1000× one
Read the last two lines together. Uncorrected, step 1 would divide a 10×-too-small numerator by a 32×-too-small denominator — a step about 3× too large, in a direction estimated from a single minibatch. Dividing each by 1−βt makes both unbiased from step 1, and the correction decays to 1 within a few hundred steps.
Hyper-parameterDefaultWhat it controls
β10.9 direction memory — 10 steps. Lower (0.8) for very noisy or very long-context data.
β20.999 / 0.95 scale memory — 1000 steps. LLM practice uses 0.95: reacts faster to loss spikes and is far more stable at large batch.
ε1e-8 not just numerical safety — it caps the maximum effective LR at η/ε for a dead coordinate. Raise to 1e-6 in bf16 or the denominator underflows.
η1e-4 – 3e-4 because the update is ≈ ±η per coordinate, this is literally the per-step change in each weight.
A useful sanity number. With η = 3×10−4 and weights of RMS ≈ 0.02, Adam moves each weight by about 1.5% of its own size per step. Over 100k steps, a weight can travel anywhere. Over 100 steps, essentially nothing happens — which is why LR sweeps on tiny budgets mislead.
m̂√v̂  ≈  𝔼[g]√𝔼[g2]  ∈  [−1, 1]
  • Bounded step. The ratio never exceeds 1, so |Δθi| ≤ η for every coordinate, always. A gradient spike of 106 produces the same step as one of 10−6.
  • It is nearly sign(g), and with β1 = β2 = 0 it is exactly −η sign(g) — which is why signSGD and Lion work nearly as well on half the state.
  • Ratio-of-moments = SNR. Near 1 where the gradient is consistent across minibatches, near 0 where it is noise: an automatic per-coordinate trust estimator.
  • Invariance. Rescale the loss, or one layer's gradients, by c and Adam's trajectory is unchanged; SGD's is not. That is the practical reason Adam trains Transformers whose layers have gradients spanning six orders of magnitude.
The flip side. Magnitude information is discarded, so Adam keeps taking η-sized steps in coordinates whose gradient is pure noise. It never settles — the schedule, not the optimiser, is what finally stops the model moving.
The whole optimiseradam.py
class AdamW:
    def __init__(self, params, lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95),
                 eps=1e-8, weight_decay=0.1):
        self.p = list(params)
        self.lr, self.eps, self.wd = lr, eps, weight_decay
        self.b1, self.b2 = betas
        self.t = 0
        self.m = [torch.zeros_like(p) for p in self.p]   # state
        self.v = [torch.zeros_like(p) for p in self.p]   # state

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self):
        self.t += 1
        bc1 = 1 - self.b1 ** self.t        # bias corrections
        bc2 = 1 - self.b2 ** self.t
        for p, m, v in zip(self.p, self.m, self.v):
            if p.grad is None: continue
            g = p.grad
            m.lerp_(g, 1 - self.b1)        # m <- b1*m + (1-b1)*g
            v.mul_(self.b2).addcmul_(g, g, value=1 - self.b2)

            denom = (v / bc2).sqrt_().add_(self.eps)
            # DECOUPLED decay: not routed through m or v
            p.mul_(1 - self.lr * self.wd)
            p.addcdiv_(m, denom, value=-self.lr / bc1)
Parameter groups — what production code doestorch.optim
decay, no_decay = [], []
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    if not p.requires_grad: continue
    # never decay biases, norm gains, or 1-D params
    if p.ndim < 2 or name.endswith(".bias"):
        no_decay.append(p)
    else:
        decay.append(p)

opt = torch.optim.AdamW(
    [{"params": decay,    "weight_decay": 0.1},
     {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0.0}],
    lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), eps=1e-8, fused=True)
On lerp_ and addcdiv_. Every line is in-place. Optimiser state is two full copies of the model; allocating a temporary per step would add a third. fused=True goes further and runs the whole update as one CUDA kernel over all parameters — typically a 10–20% end-to-end speedup on small models, where launch overhead dominates.
Why the group split matters. A LayerNorm gain initialised to 1 has no reason to be pulled toward 0: decaying it changes the function's scale, which the norm then partially undoes, leaving an unstable equilibrium. Decaying 1-D parameters is a common quiet mistake, and it costs real accuracy.

L2 regularisation (“Adam + weight_decay”)

g ← g + λθ,   Δθ = −η m̂(g + λθ)√v̂(g + λθ)

The decay term is divided by √v̂ along with everything else. A weight whose gradient is large gets a large √v and therefore less decay — the regulariser is strongest exactly where it is needed least.

Decoupled decay (AdamW)

Δθ = −η m̂(g)√v̂(g)  −  ηλθ

A clean multiplicative shrink θ ← (1−ηλ)θ, identical for every weight, independent of its gradient history. It is no longer L2 regularisation of any loss — it is a constraint on the weight norm, applied directly.

The trap in the API. torch.optim.Adam(..., weight_decay=x) gives you the top equation. torch.optim.AdamW(..., weight_decay=x) gives you the bottom one. Same argument name, different algorithm, and the useful values of λ differ by roughly η — typically 1e-2 vs 1e-1. Almost every modern recipe wants AdamW.

Warmup — the first 1–5% of steps

  • v is estimated from almost no data at small t, so 1/√v̂ has enormous variance even after bias correction. Large early steps land where the estimate is meaningless, and the run diverges or takes a permanent quality hit.
  • Initialisation puts the model at an unusually flat point (§13): gradients are small and similar across examples, so early steps are unusually large and unusually correlated.
  • The fix is trivial — ramp η linearly from 0 — and it is the difference between training and not training for post-LN Transformers (§14.5).

Decay — the remaining 95%

  • Cosine to ≈10% of peak: the default when you know the run length. Its one flaw is exactly that — the shape depends on the total step count, so you cannot extend a run.
  • WSD / trapezoid: hold η flat, then decay hard over the last 10–20%. Matches cosine's final loss, and every intermediate checkpoint can start a longer run.
  • The drop during decay is the noise ball shrinking (§10.3), not the model learning something new.
Warmup + cosine, explicitlytorch
def lr_at(t, peak=3e-4, warm=2000, total=100_000, floor=0.1):
    if t < warm:
        return peak * t / warm                    # linear ramp
    p = (t - warm) / (total - warm)               # in [0, 1]
    return peak * (floor + (1-floor) * 0.5*(1 + math.cos(math.pi*p)))

sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(opt, lambda t: lr_at(t)/3e-4)

Global-norm gradient clipping

g ← g · min(1, c‖g‖2) c = 1.0 is the near-universal default
  • Global, not per-tensor. The norm is over all parameters concatenated, so the direction of the update is exactly preserved — only its length is capped. Per-tensor clipping silently changes the direction and the relative scale between layers.
  • What it actually protects against. Not the typical step — a healthy run clips rarely. It protects against the one-in-10⁵ batch containing a pathological example whose gradient is 100× the norm, which under Adam would poison v for the next 1/(1−β2) steps.
  • Log the pre-clip norm. It is the single most informative training metric after the loss: a slow rise means instability building; a sudden spike identifies the exact batch; a flat line near c means you are clipping every step and your learning rate is really c/‖g‖ times smaller than you think.
The real calltorch.nn.utils
gn = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
if not torch.isfinite(gn):          # NaN/Inf batch: skip it
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) # do NOT let it into m, v
    continue
log("grad_norm", gn.item())

Numerics · bf16 and fp16. Keep θ, m, v and the optimiser arithmetic in fp32; use bf16/fp16 only for activations and the forward/backward matmuls. A step of 3×10−4 added to a weight of 0.02 in bf16 (8 bits of mantissa) rounds away entirely — the model silently stops learning. fp16 additionally needs a loss scaler because gradients underflow below 6×10−8; bf16 has fp32's exponent range and does not.
Memory, per parameter, mixed-precision AdamW. 4 (fp32 master θ) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) + 2 (bf16 θ) + 2 (bf16 g) = 16 bytes. A 7 B model is 112 GB of optimiser plumbing — before activations. This is the entire reason ZeRO/FSDP sharding, 8-bit Adam and Adafactor exist.
OptimiserState/paramfp32 bytesScale-invariant?Typical use in 2025
