“Scale-invariant” = the trajectory is unchanged if the loss, or one layer's gradients, are multiplied by a constant. It is the property that lets one learning rate serve every layer of a 100-layer network — and the reason the right-hand column looks the way it does.

The trade, stated plainly. Every rung of the ladder spends memory and per-step time to reduce the number of steps. Which one wins depends on whether your run is bound by steps (small model, huge data) or by memory (huge model).
Adafactor's trick. Store only the row and column means of v for an m×n weight, and reconstruct the full matrix as their outer product — O(m+n) instead of O(mn). A rank-1 approximation of the second moment turns out to be nearly free of cost in quality.
Where this is going. Note that the last row keeps one buffer, like plain momentum, and still claims scale invariance. That is not a diagonal preconditioner at all — it is §12.

Adam's P is diagonal, so it is invariant to permuting the entries of W. It therefore cannot represent anything about W's structure as a linear map — for instance, that its gradient is nearly low-rank.

And it is. Empirically the gradient of a Transformer weight matrix has a fast-decaying spectrum: a handful of singular directions carry most of the energy. The update inherits that, so a few directions move a lot and the rest barely move at all.

A weight W ∈ ℝm×n is a linear map. The size of a change to a linear map is how much it can change the output for a unit input — the spectral norm ‖ΔW‖2 = σmax, not the Frobenius norm that Adam and SGD implicitly use. Constrain that:

ΔW⋆= arg max‖ΔW‖2 ≤ η ⟨M, ΔW⟩ M = the momentum buffer M= UΣV⊤ its SVD ΔW⋆= η UV⊤ the dual norm is nuclear; equality at the “matrix sign”
Read the answer. UV⊤ is M with every singular value set to 1. Adam sets every coordinate's magnitude to η; Muon sets every singular direction's magnitude to η. It is the same idea — discard magnitude, keep direction — applied in the basis that respects what a matrix is.
Why this should help. If 90% of the momentum's energy sits in three singular directions, plain momentum spends the step there and the rest of the layer is effectively frozen. Orthogonalisation gives every direction the same budget — a full-rank update instead of a nearly rank-3 one.

An SVD per weight per step is out of the question. But we do not need U and V — only their product, which is the matrix function f(σ) = 1 applied to the spectrum. Any odd polynomial p(X) = aX + b(XX⊤)X + c(XX⊤)2X acts on X = UΣV⊤ as U p(Σ) V⊤ — it touches only the singular values. So: choose the coefficients so that iterating p pushes every σ ∈ (0,1] toward 1, and apply it five times.

Newton–Schulz, quinticmuon.py
@torch.no_grad()
def zeropower_via_newtonschulz5(G, steps=5, eps=1e-7):
    """Approximate U V^T for G = U S V^T, without an SVD.
    Coefficients tuned so the iteration converges FAST rather
    than monotonically -- sigma lands in roughly [0.7, 1.3],
    which is close enough: only the *direction* matters."""
    assert G.ndim == 2
    a, b, c = 3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315
    X = G.bfloat16()                      # bf16 is enough
    if G.size(0) > G.size(1):
        X = X.T                           # work on the short side
    X = X / (X.norm() + eps)              # ensure sigma_max <= 1

    for _ in range(steps):
        A = X @ X.T                       # (m, m)
        B = b * A + c * (A @ A)
        X = a * X + B @ X

    return X.T if G.size(0) > G.size(1) else X
The stepmuon.py
@torch.no_grad()
def muon_step(p, buf, lr, mu=0.95, wd=0.0, nesterov=True):
    g = p.grad
    buf.mul_(mu).add_(g)                       # M <- mu M + G
    g = g.add(buf, alpha=mu) if nesterov else buf

    o = zeropower_via_newtonschulz5(g)         # ~ U V^T

    # RMS-match to AdamW: UV^T has entry-RMS 1/sqrt(max(m,n))
    m, n = p.shape
    o = o * (0.2 * max(m, n) ** 0.5)

    p.mul_(1 - lr * wd).add_(o, alpha=-lr)
Why the coefficients look wrong. Classical Newton–Schulz (3/2, −1/2) converges monotonically but slowly. These are tuned to overshoot: they lift the small singular values to ≈1 in five steps, at the cost of leaving the spectrum only roughly flat. A 20% error in a singular value matters far less than getting all of them off the floor.
Cost. Ten matmuls per matrix per step — well under a percent of the forward/backward cost, at full bf16 tensor-core throughput, and shardable across ranks.

Notice what is missing: no second moment, no bias correction, no ε — the scale invariance comes from the geometry, not from an estimated magnitude.

ParameterShapeOptimiserWhy
Hidden weight matricesm×nMuongenuinely a linear map between two learned spaces
Token embeddingV×dAdamWrows are independent; gradients are extremely sparse
Output head / unembeddingd×VAdamWsame, and its scale interacts with the softmax
Norm gains, biasesdAdamW1-D — there is no spectrum to flatten
Conv kernelsco×ci×k×kMuonafter reshaping to co×(cik2)
The one-sentence recipe. Muon on every parameter with p.ndim >= 2 that is not an embedding or the output head; AdamW on the rest; one warmup–decay schedule shared by both, with the Muon learning rate roughly 10–50× the AdamW one (different units — see the RMS-matching line in the code).
Honest status, as of 2025. Muon won the NanoGPT speedrun and has been reported at scale — Moonshot's Moonlight (16 B MoE) and Kimi K2 (1 T total parameters) report training with Muon variants, and claim roughly 2× the sample efficiency of a tuned AdamW baseline. Independent replications at the largest scales are still thin, and the reported gains shrink when the AdamW baseline is tuned harder. Treat it as very promising and well-motivated, not as settled.
The reason to teach it. Muon is the clearest demonstration that “which optimiser” is really the question “in which norm do you measure a step?” — ‖·‖2 on the flattened vector gives SGD; ‖·‖∞ gives sign descent, which is nearly Adam; ‖·‖2→2 on the matrix gives Muon. Three optimisers, one derivation, three norms.
Practical gotchas.
  • Needs μ ≈ 0.95 and Nesterov; it is much more sensitive to the momentum coefficient than to η.
  • Attention logits can grow without bound; Kimi K2 pairs Muon with QK-clip for this. See §14.7 — QK-norm solves the same problem architecturally.
  • Weight decay still matters and is applied exactly as in AdamW.

Related: Shampoo and SOAP reach a similar place from the second-order side, and one reading of Muon is that it is Shampoo with the matrix roots replaced by the cheapest possible approximation. That the two lines of work converge on “flatten the spectrum of the update” is the interesting part.

For one linear layer h = Wx with i.i.d. zero-mean weights and independent inputs, variances simply multiply and add:

Var(hj) = nin∑i=1 Var(Wji) Var(xi)  =  ninσw2 Var(x)
Now stack L of them. The factor γ = ninσw2 applies once per layer: Var(h(L)) = γLVar(x). Anything but γ = 1 is an exponential.

Three ways to fail before step 1

  • All zeros (or any constant). Every unit in a layer computes the same thing and receives the same gradient, forever. The layer has one effective neuron. Randomness is not for luck — it is for symmetry breaking.
  • Too small. Activations vanish, so gradients ∂L/∂W(l) ∝ h(l−1) vanish too, and early layers never move. Loss decreases, slowly, using the last layer only.
  • Too large. With a saturating nonlinearity every unit pins at ±1 and the derivative is 0 — dead on arrival. With ReLU you get overflow, or a first step so large it lands somewhere useless. This is what an immediate NaN usually means.
The goal, stated once. Choose σw2 so that γ = 1 — the RMS of the activations, and of the gradients, is preserved layer to layer. Everything in §13 is a different answer to “which γ, given which nonlinearity and which architecture?”
Var(h(l))= ninσw2 Var(h(l−1)) forward pass ⇒ σw2= 1/nin to preserve activation scale Var(δ(l−1))= noutσw2 Var(δ(l)) backward pass uses W⊤ ⇒ σw2= 1/nout to preserve gradient scale σw2= 2nin + nout harmonic-mean compromise
The two constraints agree only for square layers. For nin = nout both give 1/n and there is nothing to compromise. The averaging matters in the funnel-shaped layers of a classifier head or an MLP's up/down projection — and in practice, using fan_in alone is usually fine, because normalisation layers (§14) repair the forward scale anyway.

Uniform form (what the paper states)

Wij ∼ U[−a, a],   a = √6 / (nin + nout) since Var[U(−a,a)] = a2/3
The assumption that breaks it. The derivation needs the nonlinearity to be linear near the origin with slope 1 — true for tanh at small activations, which is exactly the regime Glorot assumed. It is false for ReLU, which discards half the signal. That discrepancy is the entire content of the next slide.
Verify it yourself — 30 layers, tanhtorch
import torch, math

def probe(gain_sq, act, L=30, d=512, n=4096):
    h = torch.randn(n, d)
    for _ in range(L):
        W = torch.randn(d, d) * math.sqrt(gain_sq / d)
        h = act(h @ W.T)
    return h.std().item()

print(probe(1.0, torch.tanh))    # 0.0034   -- vanishes
print(probe(5/3 * 5/3, torch.tanh))  # 0.68  -- the tanh gain
print(probe(1.0, torch.relu))    # 3.1e-05  -- vanishes faster
print(probe(2.0, torch.relu))    # 0.99     -- Kaiming, flat
The habit to take from §13. Print the RMS of every layer's activations at initialisation, before you train anything. One forward pass; catches most init bugs instantly.

For z symmetric about zero, ReLU zeroes exactly half the mass:

𝔼[max(0, z)2] = ½ 𝔼[z2]  ⇒  Var(h) = ½ ninσw2 Var(hprev)
σw2 = 2nin “He normal”, fan_in mode

Restore the missing factor of 2 and the recursion is flat again. The general statement is σw2 = gain2/nin, where the gain is chosen so that the nonlinearity's output variance equals its input's.

Nonlinearitygainσw2note
linear, sigmoid11/nXavier's case
tanh5/32.78/ncompensates the squash
ReLU√22/nthe default
LeakyReLU(a)√(2/(1+a2))—interpolates
GELU, SiLU≈√2≈2/nReLU-like in practice
SELU3/41/nself-normalising by design
PyTorch's default is not Kaiming-for-ReLU. nn.Linear.reset_parameters calls kaiming_uniform_(w, a=math.sqrt(5)), which works out to W ∼ U(−1/√nin, 1/√nin), i.e. σw2 = 1/(3nin) — six times smaller than 2/nin. It is a compatibility artefact inherited from Torch7, not a recommendation. Deep nets survive it only because normalisation layers rescue the forward scale. If your model has no norm layers, initialise explicitly.
Explicit initialisationtorch.nn.init
def init_weights(m):
    if isinstance(m, (nn.Linear, nn.Conv2d)):
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight,
                                mode="fan_in",       # forward-preserving
                                nonlinearity="relu") # gain = sqrt(2)
        if m.bias is not None:
            nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)      # biases: always zero
    elif isinstance(m, (nn.LayerNorm, nn.BatchNorm2d)):
        nn.init.ones_(m.weight)         # gamma = 1
        nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)          # beta  = 0

model.apply(init_weights)

fan_in vs fan_out: fan_in preserves the forward pass, fan_out the backward. They differ only by the layer's aspect ratio, and across a whole network the products telescope — pick one and be consistent. fan_in is the usual choice.

Matching variance controls the average squared singular value of the layer-to-layer Jacobian. It says nothing about the spread — and a product of matrices whose singular values average 1 but range over [10−2, 102] still destroys most directions of the signal.

  • Orthogonal initialisation. Set W = gain · Q with Q⊤Q = I (from the QR of a Gaussian). Every singular value is exactly the gain, so the Jacobian is norm-preserving in every direction, not just on average — dynamical isometry. Provably lets very deep plain networks train, and is standard for RNN recurrent matrices, where the same matrix is applied T times and any spectral error is raised to the T-th power.
  • Identity / near-identity. For an RNN, Whh = I with ReLU (the IRNN) makes the default behaviour “copy the state forward”. The same instinct, applied to a residual branch, gives §13.5.
  • Data-dependent (LSUV). Initialise orthogonally, then push one real minibatch through and rescale each layer's weights so its output variance is exactly 1. Two lines of code; removes all the assumptions in the derivations at once.
Orthogonal, and LSUV in five linestorch
nn.init.orthogonal_(rnn.weight_hh, gain=1.0)

@torch.no_grad()
def lsuv(model, batch, target=1.0, iters=10):
    """Rescale every layer so its OUTPUT has unit variance
    on real data. Assumptions-free, costs 10 forward passes."""
    acts = {}
    hooks = [m.register_forward_hook(
                lambda mod, i, o: acts.__setitem__(mod, o))
             for m in model.modules()
             if isinstance(m, (nn.Linear, nn.Conv2d))]
    for _ in range(iters):
        model(batch)
        for m, out in acts.items():
            m.weight.mul_(target / (out.std() + 1e-8))
    for h in hooks: h.remove()
Why you rarely need any of this today. A normalisation layer (§14) enforces unit output scale at every step, not just at step 0, making the network exactly invariant to the scale of the preceding weight matrix. That is why modern architectures forgive bad initialisation — except in the two places normalisation cannot reach: the residual stream (§13.5) and the first and last layers.

Biases zero, norm gains one, norm shifts zero. The one common exception is a positive bias on an LSTM forget gate, so that it defaults to remembering — a structural prior, not a variance argument.

In a pre-norm block the branch output's scale does not depend on its input's, so variances simply add:

xl+1 = xl + Fl(xl)  ⇒  Var(xL) ≈ Var(x0) + L Var(F)
  • At L = 96 sub-layers the stream reaches the head with RMS ≈ 10× its starting value, so each block's relative contribution is only 1/√L. Without normalisation the growth is multiplicative, hence exponential.
  • GPT-2's fix. Scale the weights of the output projection of every residual branch by 1/√(2L) at init, so that each branch contributes 1/(2L) of the variance and the total is ≈2 regardless of depth. Two lines of code (§13.6).
  • Zero-init the last layer of each branch. Then F ≡ 0 at step 0 and the network starts as the identity — a shallow model that deepens itself as training proceeds. Used as zero-γ in ResNets, LayerScale in ViTs, and as the default in most diffusion U-Nets. It also makes LoRA and every adapter method work.
  • Fixup / T-Fixup / DeepNet push this further and derive depth-dependent scalings that let post-norm Transformers train at 1000 layers with no warmup.
Why this is an initialisation issue at all. The final LayerNorm would fix the scale — but not the fact that the contribution of block 1 and block 96 differ by √96 in relative magnitude at step 0. Depth-scaled init makes every block matter equally on the first step, which is what lets one learning rate serve all of them.
GPT-2 / LLaMA-style initmodel.py
class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        ...
        self.apply(self._init)
        # depth-scaled: every residual OUTPUT projection
        for name, p in self.named_parameters():
            if name.endswith("c_proj.weight"):     # attn + mlp out
                nn.init.normal_(p, mean=0.0,
                    std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * cfg.n_layer))

    def _init(self, m):
        if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.normal_(m.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
            if m.bias is not None:
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
        elif isinstance(m, nn.Embedding):
            nn.init.normal_(m.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
        elif isinstance(m, nn.LayerNorm):
            nn.init.ones_(m.weight); nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
LineReason
σ = 0.02 everywhere For d = 768, √(2/d) = 0.051 and √(1/d) = 0.036 — so 0.02 is deliberately small. Pre-LN makes the forward scale irrelevant, and starting small keeps early attention logits small and the softmax near-uniform.
1/√(2L) on c_proj §13.5 — keeps residual-stream variance O(1) at any depth. The 2 counts two residual branches per block.
Embedding ∼ N(0, 0.022) Not 1/√d: an embedding lookup is a selection, not a matmul, so there is no fan-in to preserve. Its scale sets the scale of the whole residual stream.
Weight tying If the output head shares the embedding matrix, its init is already fixed — and the logit scale becomes σ√d, which is why tied models often need a temperature or a final norm.
LayerNorm γ=1, β=0 Start as the identity transform. Never decay these (§11.5).
Scaling caveat. A fixed σ = 0.02 is not width-independent: as d grows, 0.02√d drifts, and the optimal learning rate drifts with it. Width-scaled parameterisations (μP) fix σ ∝ 1/√d and η ∝ 1/d for the hidden layers, so that a learning rate tuned on a small model transfers exactly to a large one. See §15.3.
y = γ x − μℰ√σℰ2 + ε + β ℰ = the set of entries averaged over

Every normalisation layer in deep learning is this formula. They differ only in ℰ. The learned γ, β exist so the layer can represent the identity — normalisation removes a degree of freedom, and the affine gives it back under the optimiser's control.

train:
  μc = meanN,H,W(x),   σc2 = varN,H,W(x) this batch
  y = γc(x−μc)/√σc2+ε + βc
  μrun ← (1−m)μrun + mμc EMA, m=0.1 — not used in this step
  σ2run ← (1−m)σ2run + mσc2
eval:
  y = γc(x−μrun)/√σ2run+ε + βc now a fixed affine map
This is why model.eval() exists. In train mode the output for one example depends on the other examples in its batch — the model is not a function of its input alone. In eval mode it is. Forgetting model.eval() at validation time is the single most common bug in student code, and it looks like “my model is worse on the val set” rather than like a crash.
Free bonus. At inference the normalisation is a per-channel affine map with constant coefficients, so it can be folded into the preceding convolution's weights and bias. Deployed ResNets contain no BatchNorm layers at all — it costs exactly zero at test time.
BatchNorm2d, from scratchnorm.py
class BatchNorm2d(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C, eps=1e-5, momentum=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps, self.momentum = eps, momentum
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(C))    # gamma
        self.bias   = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(C))   # beta
        # buffers, NOT parameters: saved, but never optimised
        self.register_buffer("running_mean", torch.zeros(C))
        self.register_buffer("running_var",  torch.ones(C))

    def forward(self, x):                    # x: (N, C, H, W)
        if self.training:
            mu  = x.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3))      # over N, H, W
            var = x.var(dim=(0, 2, 3), unbiased=False)
            with torch.no_grad():
                m = self.momentum
                self.running_mean.lerp_(mu,  m)
                # note: PyTorch stores the UNBIASED var here
                n = x.numel() / x.size(1)
                self.running_var.lerp_(var * n / (n - 1), m)
        else:
            mu, var = self.running_mean, self.running_var

        xhat = (x - mu[:, None, None]) / (var[:, None, None] + self.eps).sqrt()
        return xhat * self.weight[:, None, None] + self.bias[:, None, None]

Read the register_buffer lines. Running statistics are optimiser state that lives in the model — they are in state_dict(), they are not in parameters(), no gradient touches them, and they must be synchronised across ranks yourself (SyncBatchNorm) or every rank quietly holds a different model.

Why it helps

  • Scale invariance of the preceding weights. BN(aWx) = BN(Wx) for any a > 0. The function is unchanged, so the gradient obeys ∇aWL = ∇WL/a: a large weight automatically receives a small gradient. The effective learning rate becomes η/‖W‖2, which self-adjusts — this is why BN nets tolerate learning rates 10× higher and are so insensitive to initialisation scale (§13.4).
  • A smoother loss surface. Santurkar et al. (2018) showed BN improves the Lipschitz constants of both L and ∇L — i.e. it reduces κ (§9.2). They also showed that injecting covariate shift after BN does not hurt training, which is the direct refutation of the original paper's explanation.
  • Regularisation, for free. Each example's output depends on its random batch-mates, which is noise — worth roughly a Dropout layer, and part of why BN + Dropout together often underperforms either alone.

Where it breaks

SituationWhat goes wrong
Small batch (B ≤ 8) the statistics are themselves noisy; the noise is multiplicative and does not average out. Detection and segmentation models hit this constantly → GroupNorm.
Batch size 1 / onlinevariance is 0. The layer is undefined.
Distributed training each rank normalises by its own micro-batch, so the effective B is the micro-batch. Needs SyncBatchNorm, which costs an all-reduce per layer per step.
Gradient accumulationsame problem: 8×accumulation of 4 is not a batch of 32 for BN.
Variable-length sequences statistics over padded positions are meaningless, and the batch composition changes what a token maps to → nobody uses BN in a Transformer.
Train / test skew running stats are an EMA of a moving distribution; if the model changed fast at the end of training, they are stale. Fine-tuning under domain shift can require re-estimating them.
RL / non-i.i.d. batchescorrelated batch-mates make the statistics meaningless.
The summary that matters. BatchNorm is superb for large-batch i.i.d. vision training and awkward everywhere else. Every alternative in §14.4–§14.5 exists to keep the benefits while removing the dependence on the batch.

LayerNorm · Ba, Kiros & Hinton, 2016

μ = 1dd∑ixi,   yi = γi xi − μ√σ2+ε + βi

RMSNorm · Zhang & Sennrich, 2019

yi = γi xi√ 1d∑xj2 + ε no μ, no β
  • Both are per-token. For a (B, T, d) tensor the statistics are computed over d only, separately for each of the B×T positions. No batch coupling, identical in train and eval, works at B=1, works with any sequence length. That is the entire reason Transformers use them.
  • Dropping the mean costs nothing. Re-centring turned out not to matter: the useful part is fixing the scale of the residual stream. RMSNorm removes one reduction and one subtraction — roughly 7–15% of a norm layer's time, and norm layers are memory-bandwidth bound, so it shows up end-to-end. LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen and most models since 2023 use it.
  • Also drop β. A learned bias on the residual stream is redundant with the next linear layer's bias, which most modern architectures have also removed.
Both, from scratchnorm.py
class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))

    def forward(self, x):                 # x: (..., d)
        # compute in fp32: x.pow(2) in bf16 overflows/underflows
        dt = x.dtype
        x  = x.float()
        rms = x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True).add(self.eps).rsqrt()
        return (x * rms).to(dt) * self.weight

# LayerNorm, for comparison -- two extra reductions
mu  = x.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
var = x.var(-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
y   = (x - mu) * (var + eps).rsqrt() * gamma + beta
Three real bugs, in order of frequency.
  • .mean(-1) normalises the last dim — for (N,C,H,W) images that is W.
  • Statistics in bf16: squaring a 1e-3 activation underflows and the norm returns garbage. Always upcast.
  • ε inside vs outside the root — a silent mismatch when porting weights between frameworks.
Post-LNPre-LN
FormLN(x + F(x))x + F(LN(x))
Grad at layer 1decays with depth≈ unattenuated
Warmupmandatoryoptional
Depth > 24fragileroutine
Residual growthbounded by the LNgrows as L — needs §13.5
Final loss, if it trainsoften slightly betterbaseline
Needs a final LNnoyes — before the head
The mechanism, in one sentence. In Pre-LN there exists a path from the loss to layer 1 that is a pure sum of identities, so ∂L/∂x1 contains an ∞-strength term that no normalisation can shrink. In Post-LN every such path is squeezed through L normalisations, each of which divides by a quantity that grows with depth.
Three refinements you will see. DeepNorm: post-LN with a depth-dependent α on the skip, stable to 1000 layers. Sandwich norm (Gemma 2, GLM): norm both before and after each branch, capping the branch's contribution. QK-norm: RMSNorm on the query and key projections, which bounds the attention logits and eliminates the “attention-logit explosion” failure mode of large runs.
NormAverages overBatch-dep.?Train = eval?Where it is used
BatchNormN,H,W per channelyesnoConvNets, large-batch vision
LayerNormd per tokennoyesTransformers pre-2023, RNNs
RMSNormd per token, no meannoyesthe modern LLM default
GroupNormC/g,H,W per examplenoyesdetection, segmentation, diffusion U-Nets
InstanceNormH,W per example, per channelnoyesstyle transfer, some GANs
WeightNormthe weight, not the activationsnoyesRL, flows, small models
QK-normdhead on q, knoyeslarge-scale attention stability

GroupNorm with g = 1 is LayerNorm over (C,H,W); with g = C it is InstanceNorm. The whole family is one parameter.

Traps that survive the table.
  • Never weight-decay γ or β. They are 1-D and normalisation makes the rest of the layer scale-invariant, so decaying them moves an equilibrium rather than regularising (§11.5).
  • A bias before a norm does nothing. The norm subtracts the mean, which removes it. Turn bias=False on any linear or conv that feeds a LayerNorm or BatchNorm — free parameters and free FLOPs.
  • Norms change what weight decay does. Under BN it does not shrink the function — it raises the effective learning rate η/‖W‖2. That is the real mechanism behind “weight decay improves ImageNet accuracy”.
  • Statistics in fp32, always.
And the honest caveat. Normalisation-free architectures work too: NFNets match BN ResNets using scaled weight standardisation plus adaptive gradient clipping, and recent work replaces LayerNorm in Transformers with a scaled tanh. The property that matters is controlled activation scale, not the layer that provides it.
Transformer pre-training, annotatedtrain.py
# ---- architecture (Part I) + init (S5) --------------------
#   pre-RMSNorm blocks, bias=False everywhere,
#   std 0.02, residual out-projections x 1/sqrt(2L),
#   final RMSNorm before the head.

# ---- parameter groups (S3.5) ------------------------------
decay    = [p for n, p in named if p.ndim >= 2]
no_decay = [p for n, p in named if p.ndim <  2]   # norms, biases

opt = torch.optim.AdamW(
    [{"params": decay,    "weight_decay": 0.1},
     {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0.0}],
    lr=3e-4,               # S3.4: this IS the per-weight step
    betas=(0.9, 0.95),     # S3.3: beta2=0.95, not 0.999
    eps=1e-8,
    fused=True)

# ---- schedule (S3.7) --------------------------------------
warmup, total = 2000, 100_000        # warmup ~ 2% of the run
sched = LambdaLR(opt, lambda t: min(t / warmup,
        0.1 + 0.9 * 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi *
             min(1.0, (t - warmup) / (total - warmup))))))

# ---- the step (S2.5, S3.8) --------------------------------
with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    loss = model(x, y)               # fp32 master weights
loss.backward()
gn = clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
opt.step(); sched.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

Change one thing at a time. These interact: raising η and lowering β2 and lengthening warmup all mitigate the same instability, so a sweep over all three tells you almost nothing. Fix a budget, sweep η alone on a log grid, then touch the rest.
And log these four, every run. loss · pre-clip ‖g‖ · the current η · the ratio RMS(Δθ)/RMS(θ) per layer. Three of the four cost nothing and the fourth is the subject of the next slide.

If it does not train at all

  • Overfit 8 examples first. A correct model reaches ~0 loss on 8 examples in under a minute. If it cannot, the bug is in the model, the loss or the data pipeline — not the learning rate.
  • Print the RMS of every layer's activations at step 0 (§13.2). Flat across depth means the init is fine; a geometric trend across layers names the broken layer directly.
  • Print ‖g‖ per layer at step 0. All zeros below some layer means the graph is severed — a detach(), a no_grad, an in-place op, or a requires_grad=False you forgot.
  • Check the step-0 loss. Cross-entropy on V classes must start at ln V — 6.9 for 1000 classes, 10.8 for a 50k vocab. Otherwise the head or the labels are wrong.

If it trains but badly

  • Sweep η on a log grid (×3 apart) for a short budget and take the largest stable value, then back off 2×. The optimum is usually just below the divergence threshold.
  • Watch RMS(Δθ)/RMS(θ). Healthy is 10−3–10−2 and roughly equal across layers. Two orders below the rest = frozen; two above = about to diverge.
  • Loss spikes that do not recover mean the second moment was poisoned (§11.8). Lower β2, or rewind to the last checkpoint and skip the offending data.
  • Validation diverging from train is not an optimiser problem. Stop tuning η.

Tune on a 100 M model, train a 100 B one. This only works if the parameterisation is chosen so that the optimal hyper-parameters are width-independent.

  • The problem. Under the standard parameterisation, as width d grows the optimal learning rate drifts (roughly as 1/d for Adam on hidden layers), activations at initialisation change scale, and attention logits grow like √d. A configuration tuned at d = 512 is simply wrong at d = 8192.
  • μP (maximal-update parameterisation). Scale three things together: init variance ∝ 1/d, the per-layer learning rate ∝ 1/d for hidden weights (and ∝ const for embeddings and the head), and the output logits by 1/d. Then every layer's RMS(Δθ) is Θ(1) in width, and the optimal η transfers — μTransfer.
  • Depth. Less settled. Scaling residual branches by 1/√L (§13.5) is the analogous move and does approximately transfer; there are depth-μP variants that make it exact for residual nets.
  • Data / batch. Bcrit grows with model size and with training progress, so the batch size you settled on for the small model is a lower bound, not a transfer.
QuantityStandardμP
Hidden init σ21/d1/d

The unifying statement of this whole deck. μP is nothing but §13 and §11 taken seriously at once: choose the initialisation and the per-layer learning rate so that the relative change per step, RMS(Δθ)/RMS(θ), is the same number for every layer and every width. Everything else follows.
If you do nothing else. Even without full μP, the rule η ∝ 1/√d and RMSNorm-everywhere gets most of the transfer, and costs one line.

The claim Part II has been making all along. Optimisation, initialisation and normalisation are not three topics. They are three instruments pointed at one quantity, and a training run is healthy exactly when that quantity is Θ(1) everywhere — across layers, across steps, and across scales.
Carried over. Colour still encodes what kind of quantity a box is, never decoration. Parts I–II fixed four accents plus optimiser state; this part adds two.

One convention worth stating early: D counts tokens processed, so a second epoch over the same corpus doubles D. Whether those two Ds are worth the same is a live research question — §17.7.

Part I's Transformer begins with nn.Embedding(V, d). That signature quietly assumes a finite alphabet of V symbols and a total function from text to sequences over it. Natural language provides neither.

GranularityWhat breaks
Characters
or raw UTF-8 bytes		 tiny V Nothing is out of vocabulary, ever. But sequences get 4–5× longer, so attention costs 16–25× more, and the model must spend its early layers re-learning spelling.
Words
split on whitespace		 unbounded V Zipf's law guarantees an infinite tail: names, typos, code identifiers, agglutinative morphology. Every unseen word collapses to <UNK> — an irrecoverable loss of information, since no amount of training can un-erase it.
Subwords
BPE, WordPiece, Unigram		 chosen V Frequent words stay whole; rare words decompose into pieces that were themselves frequent. V is a hyperparameter, and coverage is still total.
The design goal. Compress the corpus into as few symbols as possible, subject to a fixed vocabulary budget and to never emitting <UNK>. Stated that way, this is a compression problem — which is exactly what BPE was invented for (Gage, 1994), decades before anyone applied it to translation (Sennrich et al., 2016).

Fix the body of the model at N non-embedding parameters and width d. Processing one character of text costs

c(V) = t(V) · 6(N + 2dV)

where t(V) is tokens per character — the compression rate of the tokeniser — and 2dV counts the input embedding plus the output projection.

  • t(V) falls roughly like 1/log V: doubling the vocabulary buys ever less compression, because each new merge covers a rarer string.
  • 2dV grows linearly, and it is pure width — a token seen 40 times in the corpus gets 40 gradient updates for its embedding row.
In practice. The product is remarkably flat between 3×104 and 2×105, which is why every modern model sits there: GPT-2 50 257, Llama 2 32 000, Llama 3 128 256, Gemma 256 000. Multilingual models push right, because t(V) for their corpus is much worse at small V.

The choice is irreversible: V is baked into the embedding shape on step 0, and changing it invalidates every checkpoint.

Training (learning the merge list)
  1. Initialise the vocabulary with the 256 possible bytes. Every string is now representable, so <UNK> is structurally impossible.
  2. Count every adjacent pair of symbols in the corpus, weighted by how often it occurs.
  3. Merge the most frequent pair (a, b): append ab to the vocabulary, append (a, b) to the ordered merge list, and rewrite every occurrence.
  4. Repeat from 2 until the vocabulary reaches V.

That is the entire method. There is no objective function, no gradient, and no probability model — BPE is a greedy compression heuristic, and its only justification is that it works.

The artefact is the list, not the vocabulary. Two tokenisers with identical vocabularies but different merge orders segment text differently. The ordered list is the model; the vocabulary is a by-product.

Relatives worth knowing: WordPiece merges the pair maximising p(ab)/p(a)p(b) rather than raw count; Unigram LM (SentencePiece) starts from a large vocabulary and prunes by marginal likelihood, which gives it a real probability over segmentations.

Read the trace as a policy. Frequent whole words (newest␣) become single tokens. Rare words are left as their frequent parts (low·e·r␣). The vocabulary spends its budget exactly where the corpus spends its mass.
Naive BPE trainingO(V · W · L)
from collections import Counter

def merge_word(w, pair):
    """Rewrite one symbol tuple, left to right."""
    a, b, out, i = *pair, [], 0
    while i < len(w):
        if i < len(w) - 1 and w[i] == a and w[i+1] == b:
            out.append(a + b); i += 2      # consume BOTH
        else:
            out.append(w[i]); i += 1
    return tuple(out)

def train_bpe_naive(word_freqs, n_merges):
    """word_freqs: {symbol_tuple: corpus count}."""
    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        pairs = Counter()
        for w, f in word_freqs.items():        # rescan the whole corpus
            for p in zip(w, w[1:]):
                pairs[p] += f
        if not pairs:
            break
        best = max(pairs, key=lambda p: (pairs[p], p))
        merges.append(best)
        word_freqs = {merge_word(w, best): f   # rewrite the whole corpus
                      for w, f in word_freqs.items()}
    return merges
One real optimisation is already here. The corpus is stored as word types with counts, not as a stream. Zipf's law is generous: 15 TB of English text contains only ≈107 distinct pre-tokens, so this alone is a 105× reduction before any cleverness.
And two disasters remain. Both loops in the body touch every word type, every merge:
  • Recounting is O(W̄L) per merge, but a merge changes the count of at most a handful of pairs.
  • Rewriting allocates a fresh tuple for every word, including the >99.9% that do not contain the merged pair.
107
word types W
5×104
merges V
1013
symbol visits

At a very optimistic 108 Python symbol-visits per second that is ≈3 years. The algorithm is not wrong; the data structures are.

Merging (a, b) at one position destroys exactly two pairs and creates exactly two:

… x a b y …  →  … x ab y …
destroyedcreated
(x, a)(x, ab)
(b, y)(ab, y)

So the recount is O(1) per occurrence — if we can answer three questions in O(1):

  1. Which pair is largest?
    a max-heap keyed by count, with lazy deletion: never remove a stale entry, just re-push on change and discard on pop if the key disagrees with the live count.
  2. Where does this pair occur?
    an inverted index where[pair] → {(word, position)}, so a merge visits only the words that actually contain it.
  3. Who are my neighbours now?
    each word is a doubly linked list over its symbol array, so a splice is a pointer write, not a reallocation.
Build the indices oncetrain_bpe.py
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

def train_bpe(word_freqs, n_merges):
    """word_freqs: {symbol_tuple: count} -> ordered merges."""
    words = [list(w) for w in word_freqs]     # mutable symbols
    freq  = list(word_freqs.values())
    nxt = [list(range(1, len(w)+1)) for w in words]   # j -> right
    prv = [list(range(-1, len(w)-1)) for w in words]  # j -> left

    count = defaultdict(int)                  # pair -> total freq
    where = defaultdict(set)                  # pair -> {(word, j)}
    for i, w in enumerate(words):
        for j in range(len(w) - 1):
            count[w[j], w[j+1]] += freq[i]
            where[w[j], w[j+1]].add((i, j))

    heap = [(-c, p) for p, c in count.items()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)                       # (-count, pair)

    def bump(p, occ, d):        # keep all three in sync
        count[p] += d
        where[p].add(occ) if d > 0 else where[p].discard(occ)
        if count[p] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-count[p], p))   # lazy
… then only ever touch what changedtrain_bpe.py
    merges = []
    while heap and len(merges) < n_merges:
        negc, pair = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if -negc != count[pair] or count[pair] <= 0:
            continue                     # stale entry -- drop it
        merges.append(pair)
        a, b = pair
        for i, j in sorted(where.pop(pair)):   # left to right
            w, f, k = words[i], freq[i], nxt[i][j]
            if w[j] != a or k >= len(w) or w[k] != b:
                continue        # an earlier splice ate this one
            l, r = prv[i][j], nxt[i][k]
            if l >= 0:                   # (x,a) -> (x,ab)
                bump((w[l], a),   (i, l), -f)
                bump((w[l], a+b), (i, l), +f)
            if r < len(w):               # (b,y) -> (ab,y)
                bump((b,   w[r]), (i, k), -f)
                bump((a+b, w[r]), (i, j), +f)
            w[j], w[k] = a + b, None     # splice j <- k
            nxt[i][j] = r
            if r < len(w):
                prv[i][r] = j
        count[pair] = 0
    return merges
The guard is not optional. In a a a the pair (a,a) occurs at 0 and 1; merging at 0 consumes 1. Every overlapping-pair bug lives on that line.
NaiveFast
select best pair O(W̄L) full recount O(log P) heap pop
find occurrences O(W) scan every word O(1) index lookup
apply one merge O(W̄L) rebuild all O(occ) splice
total, V merges O(V · W̄L) O(W̄L + M log P)

W word types, L̄ mean length, P live pairs, M total merge events — and M < W̄L, because every event permanently removes one symbol from the corpus. The whole run is therefore near-linear in the corpus, independent of V.

The three tricks that make it production-grade.
  • Pre-tokenise first (§16.9). Merges never cross word boundaries, which caps L̄ and lets the corpus be deduplicated at all.
  • Shard and count in parallel. The initial pair census is an embarrassingly parallel map-reduce over documents; only the merge loop is sequential.
  • Write it in Rust. The loop is pointer-chasing over small integers — the worst possible case for a Python interpreter. tokenizers and tiktoken both do exactly this.

Run BPE on raw text and it will happily learn "␣of␣the" as one token, or merge across a sentence boundary. Every real tokeniser first splits the text with a hand-written regex, and only then applies merges within each piece.

The GPT-2 pattern, still in useregex
import regex as re     # not `re`: we need \p{L}

PAT = re.compile(r"""'s|'t|'re|'ve|'m|'ll|'d"""
                 r"""| ?\p{L}+| ?\p{N}+"""
                 r"""| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+""")

def pre_tokenize(text):
    return PAT.findall(text)
  •  ?\p{L}+ — a run of letters, with its leading space. This is why ␣token and token are different ids.
  • \p{N}+ is separate, so digits never merge with letters. Llama 3 goes further and caps digit runs at three, which measurably improves arithmetic.
  • \s+(?!\S) keeps a trailing run of whitespace together — the fix that lets a code model represent 16 spaces of indentation in one token.
Why it also makes things fast. Pieces are short and repetitive, so encoding can be memoised per piece and the corpus can be deduplicated into word types. The regex is a performance decision as much as a linguistic one.
One string, four stages

“Don't ␣␣␣stop”

Don't␣␣␣␣stop

The apostrophe clitic 't is its own rule; the three-space run is held together by \s+(?!\S); the final space attaches forward onto stop.

Encode one pre-tokenencode.py
from functools import lru_cache
INF = float("inf")

RANKS = {}    # {(a, b): position in the merge list}
VOCAB = {}    # {symbol bytes: token id}

@lru_cache(maxsize=1 << 20)      # Zipf makes this >99% hits
def bpe(piece):
    sym = [bytes([c]) for c in piece.encode("utf-8")]
    while len(sym) > 1:
        best = min(zip(sym, sym[1:]),
                   key=lambda p: RANKS.get(p, INF))
        if best not in RANKS:
            break                # no merge applies: done
        a, b, out, i = *best, [], 0
        while i < len(sym):
            if i < len(sym)-1 and (sym[i], sym[i+1]) == best:
                out.append(a + b); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(sym[i]); i += 1
        sym = out
    return sym

def encode(text):
    return [VOCAB[s] for piece in pre_tokenize(text)
                     for s in bpe(piece)]
Why lowest rank, not most frequent? The merge list is a replay log. Merge #2 was learned on a corpus where merge #1 had already been applied, so applying them out of order produces symbols the trainer never saw. Rank order is the only order that reproduces training-time segmentation.
StepSymbols
bytes
newest
rank 1 · (e,s)
newest
rank 2 · (es,t)
newest
rank 7 · (ne,w)
newest
rank 8 · (new,est)
newest
Cost. O(n2) in the length of one piece — which is fine, because the regex guarantees n ≲ 20 bytes and the cache means most pieces are computed once per process. tiktoken keeps the same algorithm and wins by moving it to Rust, replacing the list rebuild with an in-place rank array, and encoding document chunks in parallel.
SymptomCause, and the fix
Arithmetic fails on some numbers 1000 is one token but 1,000 is four, and 2024 may be a single frequent token while 2027 splits. Digits have no consistent positional identity. Fix: force digit runs of length 1 or 3.
Cannot count letters or reverse a word The model never sees characters — only opaque ids. Asking how many rs are in strawberry asks it to introspect a lookup table it was never shown.
Non-English costs 3× more A vocabulary trained on English-dominated data leaves other scripts near their raw UTF-8 byte length. Same context window, one third of the text, and three times the API bill.
“Glitch” tokens Strings frequent in the tokeniser corpus but scrubbed from the training corpus get a vocabulary row whose embedding is essentially at initialisation. Feeding one produces confidently strange output.
A trailing space breaks a prompt Spaces attach forward. A prompt ending in "␣" asks the model to continue a token that never begins a word in training.
And you cannot change it later. V fixes the embedding shape; the merge list fixes what every id means. Swapping the tokeniser after pre-training invalidates the checkpoint, the data pipeline and every scaling-law fit measured on it. It is the one decision in this lecture with no gradient and no undo.

Train a family of models across four orders of magnitude of size and data. Plot final loss against N, D and C on log–log axes. The points fall on straight lines — not approximately, but over seven decades.

L(X) ≈ ( XcX )αX a power law: log L is linear in log X
  • Smooth. No thresholds, no phase changes in the loss itself. Doubling the budget buys a fixed decrement in log-loss, forever — or at least as far as anyone has measured.
  • Architecture-insensitive. Depth, width and aspect ratio barely move the line as long as the parameter count is held fixed. Shape matters far less than size.
  • Predictive. This is the point. GPT-4's loss was reported as predicted from runs using 10−4 of its compute.
What it does not claim. Nothing about downstream capability. Cross-entropy on held-out text is smooth; the accuracy of a benchmark that thresholds that distribution need not be. Most reported “emergence” is a discontinuous metric on top of a continuous loss.

Take any weight w in a matrix multiply. For one token:

PassFLOPs / weightWhat it computes
forward 2 one multiply and one add into the output accumulator
backward · input 2 ∂L/∂x, to keep the chain rule going
backward · weight 2 ∂L/∂w, the thing we actually wanted
C ≈ 6 N D FLOPs

Backward costs twice forward, not once: every layer must produce two gradients, one for its input and one for its weights. This is the single most useful number in the whole lecture — it is how a GPU-hour budget becomes a number of tokens.

What the approximation drops. Attention's QK⊤ and AV products, which cost ≈ 12 Lℓd n per token and are parameter-free. They are negligible while n ≪ 12d and dominate when the context is long — at d=4096 the crossover is around 50k tokens of context. Activation recomputation adds another ≈1ND, which is why practitioners often quote 8ND for real wall-clock.

Chinchilla parametric form (Hoffmann et al., 2022)

L(N, D) = E▁▁entropy of text + ANα▁▁▁model too small + BDβ▁▁▁data too little
TermFittedReading
E≈ 1.69 the loss of a perfect model with infinite data — the entropy of natural text under this tokeniser
A, α406, 0.34 approximation error: a finite Transformer cannot express the true conditional
B, β411, 0.28 estimation error from finite data — Part I's εest, now measured
Recognise the decomposition. This is exactly the approximation / estimation split from Part I slide 6, with numbers attached. α ≈ β is the important fact: the two terms fall at nearly the same rate, so neither resource should be starved. Any allocation that grows one much faster than the other wastes the other.

Minimise the loss subject to a fixed budget:

minN,D  E + A N−α + B D−β   s.t.   6ND = C
ℒ= A N−α + B D−β + λ(6ND − C) the Lagrangian ∂ℒ/∂N= −αA N−α−1 + 6λD = 0 ∂ℒ/∂D= −βB D−β−1 + 6λN = 0 λ⇒ αA N−α = βB D−β eliminate λ; multiply by N and D
The balance condition. At the optimum the two error terms sit in a fixed ratio β/α — neither goes to zero, and you buy them down together. That is the whole content of Chinchilla.

Substitute D = C/6N and solve: the exponents opposite must sum to 1, since ND ∝ C.

The compute-optimal frontier

Nopt = G (C6)a,   Dopt = G−1 (C6)b
a = βα+β,   b = αα+β,   G = (αAβB)1/(α+β)

Three independent estimates — 0.50, 0.49, and β/(α+β) ≈ 0.45 — are the honest error bar.

Read the exponents. a ≈ b ≈ 0.5 says: given 100× the compute, make the model 10× bigger and train on 10× more tokens. Kaplan's 0.73/0.27 says make it 27× bigger on 3.7× the data — which is precisely what the field did from 2020 to 2022, and precisely why GPT-3 at 175B parameters on 300B tokens was badly undertrained.
175B / 300B
GPT-3 · ratio 1.7
70B / 1.4T
Chinchilla · ratio 20

Chinchilla is 2.5× smaller than GPT-3, cost the same to train, and beat it on essentially everything.

Three approaches, one answer

  • Fix model, vary data. Read the minimum-envelope of many loss curves. Cheap, but conflates “stopped early” with “too small”.
  • IsoFLOP profiles (above). The cleanest: each parabola is an honest controlled experiment at fixed C.
  • Fit the parametric form to all runs at once and differentiate. Most data-efficient, most sensitive to the fit.
Why Kaplan got a different answer. Two methodological details, both invisible at the time:
  • The learning-rate schedule was not re-tuned per run, so the cosine decay did not end when the token budget did. Under-decayed runs look artificially bad at large D — which biases the fit toward “data does not help, buy parameters”.
  • Embedding parameters were excluded inconsistently, distorting small-model points.

The lesson generalises: an extrapolation inherits every confound of the runs it was fitted to. Chinchilla's own fit has been re-examined since — exponents robust, constants less so.

Fit L(N, D) to a sweep of small runsscaling.py
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

def log_loss_pred(p, N, D):
    """Huber-fit in log space: the paper's parameterisation
       e, a, b are logs of E, A, B -> positivity for free."""
    e, a, b, alpha, beta = p
    return np.logaddexp.reduce(np.stack([
        np.full_like(N, e),
        a - alpha * np.log(N),
        b - beta  * np.log(D),
    ]), axis=0)

def huber(r, delta=1e-3):
    return np.where(np.abs(r) < delta,
                    0.5 * r**2, delta * (np.abs(r) - 0.5*delta))

def fit(N, D, L):
    obj = lambda p: huber(log_loss_pred(p, N, D)
                          - np.log(L)).sum()
    best = min((minimize(obj, x0, method="L-BFGS-B")
                for x0 in np.random.randn(40, 5) * 2),
               key=lambda r: r.fun)          # multi-start
    return best.x

Fitting in log space with a Huber loss is not cosmetic: a plain least-squares fit on L is dominated by the smallest, noisiest runs.

Turn the fit into a planscaling.py
def allocate(p, C):
    """Compute-optimal (N, D) for a budget of C FLOPs."""
    e, a, b, alpha, beta = p
    A, B = np.exp(a), np.exp(b)
    G = (alpha * A / (beta * B)) ** (1 / (alpha + beta))
    N = G * (C / 6) ** (beta / (alpha + beta))
    return N, (C / 6) / N

C = 1024 * 8 * 4.0e14 * 3600 * 24 * 30    # ~1e24 FLOPs
N, D = allocate(p_hat, C)
print(f"{N/1e9:.0f}B params, {D/1e12:.1f}T tokens")
Sanity checks before you spend the money.
  • Does the fit reproduce a held-out larger run? If it cannot predict 10×, it will not predict 1000×.
  • Is D even available? A 20:1 plan for a 400B model needs 8T tokens you have rights to.
  • Does the model fit and serve? §18–§19 are why the answer is often no.

Chinchilla minimises training FLOPs for a target loss. If the model will then serve 1015 tokens of inference, that is the wrong objective. Add the serving term:

Ctotal = 6NDtrain + 2N Dinf 2 FLOPs/param/token, forward only

Minimising this under a loss constraint pushes N down and D up, sometimes far past 20:1. The training run gets more expensive; every inference call gets cheaper forever.

ModelNDD/N
GPT-3175B0.3T1.7
Chinchilla70B1.4T20
Llama 27B2T286
Llama 38B15T1875

Llama 3 8B is roughly 100× past “compute-optimal”. Its loss is worse than a Chinchilla-optimal model trained on the same FLOPs — and it is the far better product, because it runs on one GPU.

Three places the law bends
  • Data runs out. Repeating data is not free but is not worthless: up to roughly 4 epochs, repeated tokens are worth nearly as much as fresh ones; past ≈16 they add almost nothing. (Muennighoff et al., 2023)
  • Sparsity changes the exponents. An MoE has two sizes — total and active — and its scaling law needs both. §18.
  • Quality beats quantity. The constants A, B, E are properties of the corpus. Deduplication and filtering move the whole curve down, which no amount of compute can do.
What survives. The exponents are not the takeaway. The takeaway is the method: measure a family of cheap runs, fit a smooth surface, differentiate under your real constraint — whether that constraint is training FLOPs, serving cost, memory, or tokens you are allowed to use. The frontier moves; the procedure does not.

And note what §17 has not given us: a way to make a model with more parameters without paying for them at every token. That is §18.

Everything so far assumes the dense identity FLOPs/token = 2N. Section 17 says loss falls with N; it also says the bill rises with N. Those are the same N.

The observation. They need not be. Nothing in a Transformer requires every token to consult every weight. Split the feed-forward block into E parallel copies — experts — and route each token to k ≪ E of them. Parameters scale with E; FLOPs scale with k.
Ntotal ∝ E     Nactive ∝ k the two sizes an MoE has

Why should this work at all? Because the FFN is where a Transformer stores knowledge, and knowledge is sparsely accessed: the weights that know about Cantonese grammar are dead weight on a Python token. Attention, which does routing between positions, is dense and stays dense.

What you pay instead. Memory (all E experts must be resident), network traffic (§18.6), and a new failure mode that does not exist in dense models — the router can collapse (§18.4).

The whole thing, in three lines

s = softmax(Wrx) router logits → probabilities, Wr ∈ ℋE×d
𝒦 = TopK(s, k) the indices of the k largest — not differentiable, and that is fine
y = ∑i∈𝒦 si∑j∈𝒦 sj  Ei(x) renormalised gate × expert output
  • Each expert is an ordinary FFN. Ei(x) = W2(i) σ(W1(i)x). No new mathematics — Part I's MLP, replicated.
  • The gate value si multiplies the output. This is the only path by which the router receives gradient: if expert i's output helped, ∂L/∂si pushes its logit up. Routing is learned indirectly, through the usefulness of what it selected.
  • Only the top k are computed. Experts outside 𝒦 receive no gradient at all this step — the source of every instability in §18.4.

Variants worth naming: softmax-then-topk (above, Switch/Mixtral) versus topk-then-softmax; sigmoid gates instead of softmax (DeepSeek-V3), which decouple the experts' scores from each other and behave better at large E.

Routing and dispatchmoe.py
class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, hidden, n_exp=8, k=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.k = k
        self.router  = nn.Linear(d, n_exp, bias=False)
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList(
            FFN(d, hidden) for _ in range(n_exp))

    def forward(self, x):                 # x: (B, T, d)
        B, T, d = x.shape
        x = x.reshape(-1, d)              # (tokens, d)

        logits = self.router(x)                    # (tok, E)
        probs  = logits.softmax(-1)
        w, idx = probs.topk(self.k, dim=-1)        # (tok, k)
        w = w / w.sum(-1, keepdim=True)            # renormalise

        y = torch.zeros_like(x)
        for e, expert in enumerate(self.experts):
            tok, slot = (idx == e).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
            if tok.numel() == 0:
                continue                  # nobody chose this expert
            out = expert(x[tok])          # GATHER, then one dense matmul
            y.index_add_(0, tok, out * w[tok, slot, None])

        return y.reshape(B, T, d), probs, idx
Read x[tok] carefully. That gather is the entire trick. Tokens routed to expert e are collected into one contiguous batch, so the expert runs as a single dense GEMM at full efficiency. Sparsity lives in the indexing, never in the arithmetic — GPUs are catastrophically bad at genuinely sparse matmuls.
LineWhy it is there
w / w.sum(...) keeps the output scale independent of how confident the router happened to be
index_add_ scatters results back; a token picked by two experts accumulates both, weighted
return probs, idx the load-balancing loss of §18.4 needs them — it is computed outside the layer
Why this exact code is slow. The Python loop over experts serialises E small kernels, and nonzero forces a device sync. Production kernels replace the whole body with one sort by expert id, a grouped GEMM over variable-sized blocks, and a fused scatter. The semantics above are exactly right; only the schedule changes.
The positive feedback loop. An expert that is chosen slightly more often gets slightly more gradient, becomes slightly better, and is therefore chosen more often still. Left alone, a handful of experts absorb nearly all traffic and the rest never train — you have paid for E experts and received three.

Auxiliary load-balancing loss

Laux = α E E∑i=1 fi Pi

fi = fraction of tokens in the batch dispatched to expert i (a hard count — no gradient); Pi = mean router probability for expert i (smooth — carries the gradient).

The product is minimised when both are uniform, and its gradient flows through Pi only: an overloaded expert's logits get pushed down in proportion to how overloaded it actually was. Typical α ≈ 10−2 — large enough to balance, small enough not to fight the language-modelling objective.

A second term, the router z-loss (1/T)∑t(log ∑i ezi)2, keeps the logits small. It costs nothing and removes most of the remaining instability: the router is the one place where an overflow changes which computation happens, not just its value.

Expert capacity

Kernels want fixed shapes; routing does not. So each expert gets a buffer:

capacity = γ · k · tokensE γ = capacity factor, typically 1.0–1.25
  • γ too small → overflow. Excess tokens are dropped: the expert is skipped, the residual carries them, and nothing reports an error.
  • γ too large → padded buffers: wasted FLOPs and wasted bandwidth on zeros.
At inference, drop nothing. Dropping is a tolerable regulariser in training; while serving it makes a reply depend on which other requests share the batch.
The two auxiliary termsmoe.py
def aux_losses(probs, idx, n_exp, k, alpha=1e-2, beta=1e-3):
    tok = probs.size(0)
    f = torch.bincount(idx.flatten(),
                       minlength=n_exp).float() / (tok * k)
    P = probs.mean(0)                       # (E,) differentiable
    balance = alpha * n_exp * (f * P).sum()
    z = beta * probs.logsumexp(-1).pow(2).mean()
    return balance + z

Auxiliary-loss-free balancing (DeepSeek-V3, 2024)

The balancing loss has a real cost: it is a second objective pulling the router away from the routing that would minimise perplexity. The alternative is to balance without touching the gradient at all.

𝒦 = TopK(s + b, k) bias steers selection
gate = si but the gate is the unbiased score

After each step, nudge the bias by a constant γ against the observed load:

No gradient involved — a control loopmoe.py
@torch.no_grad()
def update_bias(bias, load, k, tok, gamma=1e-3):
    target = tok * k / bias.numel()
    bias += gamma * torch.sign(target - load)   # over -> down
Why this is better. The bias affects which experts are chosen but never how much their outputs count, so the language-modelling gradient is left alone. Balance becomes a feedback controller sitting outside the optimiser rather than a competing term inside the loss — the same move as decoupling weight decay in Part II's AdamW.
1 · Fine-grained experts
Split each expert into m narrower ones and raise k to mk. Parameters and FLOPs are unchanged — but the number of possible routing combinations explodes from C(E, k) to C(mE, mk).
C(16, 2) = 120  →  C(64, 8) ≈ 4.4×109

More ways to combine knowledge, at identical cost. DeepSeek-V3 takes this to 256 routed experts with k=8.

2 · Shared experts
Reserve one or two experts that every token uses, unrouted. They absorb the common knowledge — syntax, formatting, high-frequency words — that every routed expert would otherwise have to duplicate.
y = Eshared(x) + ∑i∈𝒦 gi Ei(x)

Frees the routed experts to actually specialise, and gives every token a guaranteed dense path — useful when routing is noisy early in training.

ResourceDenseMoE, E experts, top-k
FLOPs / token 2N ≈ 2N — unchanged
Parameters N ≈ E/k × N
Memory (weights + optimiser) 16N bytes 16 · E/k · N bytes
Network / layer none extra two all-to-all collectives
Failure modes — collapse, dropped tokens, stragglers
The all-to-all is the real tax. Tokens live on the device that holds their sequence; experts live on the device that holds their weights. Every MoE layer must therefore ship each token's activation to k other devices and ship the results back. That is 2k hidden vectors per token per layer crossing the network, and it is why MoE training is bandwidth-bound in a way dense training is not.

It is also why k is small and why experts are placed to keep all-to-all inside a node where possible — a theme §19 will make explicit.

Modeltotalactive Ek

DeepSeek-V3 '24671B37B256+18

Note the trajectory: a handful of wide experts in 2021; many narrow experts plus a shared one, with k=8, by 2024. The combinatorial argument of §18.6 won.

Does MoE beat dense at equal compute?
Yes, consistently, at equal training FLOPs — an MoE reaches a given loss with roughly 2–7× less compute than a dense model, with the gain growing as E grows and shrinking as the budget grows.

But it is not free at equal memory, at equal serving cost per user, or at equal engineering effort. The honest summary: MoE converts a memory-and-bandwidth surplus into a compute saving. If you have that surplus, take it.

Section 18 in one line. MoE decouples Ntotal from Nactive — and hands the bill to the interconnect, which is exactly what §19 is about.

Mixed-precision training with Adam stores six things per parameter, only one of which is the parameter you think about:

bytes per parameter — total 16

ModelNstates80GB GPUs, weights alone
Llama 3 8B8B128 GB2

And that is before activations. A batch of B sequences of length n stores ≈ Lℓ Bnd activations per saved tensor for the backward pass — often larger than the weights. Activation checkpointing trades this for compute: keep only layer boundaries, recompute the interiors during backward, paying ≈33% more FLOPs to cut activation memory by ≈an order of magnitude. It is orthogonal to everything else in §19 and almost always on.

Replicate the model on every device, give each a slice of the batch, and average the gradients before stepping:

g = 1P P∑p=1 g(p) one all-reduce of 2N bytes per step

Ring all-reduce moves 2(P−1)/P ≈ 2 times the gradient size per device regardless of P, and overlaps with the backward pass — bucket the gradients and launch each all-reduce as soon as its layer's backward finishes. Done properly, data parallelism is nearly free in time.

But it is not free in memory. Every device stores the same 16 bytes/parameter. At P=1024 the cluster holds 1024 identical copies of the optimiser state. That is the observation ZeRO exploits: those copies are only needed transiently.
StageShardedbytes / paramcomm
DDPnothing162Ψ
ZeRO-1optimiser states4 + 12/P2Ψ
ZeRO-2+ gradients2 + 14/P2Ψ
ZeRO-3 / FSDP+ parameters16/P3Ψ
Attention splits even more naturally. Give each device a disjoint set of heads. Heads are independent by construction, so Q, K, V projections split by column, the output projection splits by row, and again one all-reduce closes the block.
Per transformer blockcollectives
forward2 all-reduce
backward2 all-reduce
bytes each2Bnd
Why TP stops at 8. Those all-reduces are on the critical path — nothing overlaps them, because the next layer needs the result. They are only affordable over NVLink inside one node. Cross a slower link and tensor parallelism collapses; every real recipe sets dtp ≤ GPUs per node.

Sequence parallelism is the standard companion: in the LayerNorm and dropout regions between the two all-reduces, activations are also split along the sequence axis. The all-reduce becomes a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather — identical bytes, but activation memory drops by dtp×.

The bubble

bubble = P − 1m m = microbatches per step

A pipeline stage cannot start until its predecessor produces something. With P stages, the first P−1 microbatch-slots and the last are idle. The only cure is more microbatches — which needs a large global batch, which Part II told us costs learning-rate headroom.

  • Interleaved 1F1B gives each device v non-contiguous chunks of layers, cutting the bubble to (P−1)/(mv) at the cost of v× more point-to-point messages.
  • Zero-bubble schedules split the backward pass into its input-gradient and weight-gradient halves — only the first is on the critical path — and fill the gaps with the second.
Why bother at all? Pipeline traffic is one point-to-point send of the boundary activations — per stage boundary, not per layer, and it overlaps. It is the cheapest way to cross a slow network, which is why this axis spans nodes.
All-to-all is the awkward collective. Unlike all-reduce it has no ring algorithm that hides latency, its message sizes are data-dependent, and it appears twice in every MoE layer. On a 256-expert model it can be 20–40% of step time if placed carelessly.

How practitioners tame it

  • Keep it inside a node. Choose dep so that most dispatches stay on NVLink. DeepSeek-V3 constrains the router so each token reaches at most a fixed number of nodes, not just experts.
  • Overlap. Dispatch microbatch i+1 while computing microbatch i's experts. With enough microbatches the all-to-all disappears behind the GEMMs entirely.
  • Balance ruthlessly. §18.4's histogram is not about fairness; it is about the straggler that sets the step time for 1000 GPUs.
  • Send less. Dispatch activations in fp8 — they are consumed immediately by a GEMM that would have cast them anyway.

Note that expert parallelism composes with data parallelism rather than replacing it: the same device holds a shard of the experts and a slice of the batch, and the router decides which combination talks to which.

AxisTraffic per stepOverlappable?Put it
tensor 4 all-reduce / block, 2Bnd each no — critical path inside a node
expert 2 all-to-all / MoE layer partly inside a node
pipeline 1 send / stage boundary yes across nodes
data 1 all-reduce / step, 2N yes outermost
Declaring the meshtorch.distributed
mesh = init_device_mesh(
    "cuda", (8, 4, 8),                    # 256 GPUs
    mesh_dim_names=("dp", "pp", "tp"))

model = parallelize_module(model, mesh["tp"], TP_PLAN)
model = pipeline(model, mesh["pp"], n_micro=32)
model = fully_shard(model, mesh=mesh["dp"])   # ZeRO-3
The order of the mesh dimensions is the design. tp varies fastest, so its ranks are adjacent on NVLink; dp varies slowest, so its all-reduce is the one crossing the datacentre. Reverse them and the identical model trains three times slower.
  1. Turn on activation checkpointing and mixed precision. Free memory before spending devices on it.
  2. Find the smallest dtp that makes one layer fit, capped at the GPUs per node. TP is the only axis that shrinks a single layer, so it is the first resort and the most expensive one.
  3. Add pipeline stages until the whole model fits. Choose microbatches m ≥ 4P so the bubble stays under 25%, and use interleaved 1F1B if the global batch will not allow that.
  4. Shard the rest with ZeRO/FSDP over the remaining devices; this recovers the memory that replication wasted.
  5. Fill the cluster with data parallelism — but stop before the global batch exceeds what Part II's learning-rate schedule can absorb. Beyond that point, more devices buy nothing.
  6. For MoE, place dep inside the node and balance the router before blaming the network.
The constraint that ends the argument. Global batch = ddp × m × microbatch. Every axis you add changes it, and Part II showed that batch size is not a free parameter. Parallelism and optimisation are the same design problem.
Model FLOPs Utilisation — the number that matters
MFU = 6ND / step-timeP · peak FLOP/s

The fraction of the hardware you actually bought. A well-tuned dense run reaches 40–55%; a large MoE run is doing well at 30–40%. Everything in §19 is an attempt to keep this number from collapsing — and it is measured, never assumed.

SymptomUsual cause

Section 19 in one line. There is no parallelism strategy, only a mapping from four orthogonal cuts onto a hierarchy of wires — and the right mapping is the one where nothing sits on the critical path that could have been hidden behind a GEMM.
Section The question The mechanism What it costs The failure if you get it wrong

§17 Scaling laws how big, on how much data, for this budget? C≈6ND; fit L=E+AN−α+BD−β; minimise under the constraint a sweep of small runs, and the discipline to believe the extrapolation GPT-3: a model 2.5× too large, trained on 5× too little, at the same price as something better
§18 Mixture of Experts can parameters be bought without FLOPs? route each token to k of E FFNs; balance with an auxiliary loss or a bias controller E/k× the memory, and two all-to-alls per layer router collapse: you paid for 256 experts and trained 6
§19 Parallelism how is the run mapped onto the cluster? four orthogonal cuts — batch, matrix, layer stack, experts — assigned to a hierarchy of wires communication on the critical path, and a global batch you no longer control MFU of 12% — the same science, at four times the price and four times the wall-clock
The thread through all four. Each section takes a quantity the model treats as a constant — the alphabet, the parameter count, the cost per token, the device — and makes it a variable to be optimised under a budget. That reframing, not any single formula, is the engineering content of scale.
And what has not changed since Part I. It is still θ⋆ = arg min R̂(θ), still fitted by the gradient descent of Part II, still a stack of the blocks from Part I. Nothing in Part III is a new kind of model. All of it is a new kind of constraint.
